items.title: Pretreatment cognitive screening, treatment tolerability, and early mortality in older adults with advanced cancer initiating systemic therapy
items.authors: Mohamed M, Magnuson A, Chen Y, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Abnormal cognitive screening is common among older adults, yet its implications for cancer treatment tolerability remain unclear. We evaluated the association between pretreatment cognitive screening, treatment tolerability, and mortality among older adults with advanced cancer initiating systemic therapy. Methods: This is a secondary analysis of the usual-care arm of the GAP70+ cluster-randomized clinical trial (NCT02054741). Participants were adults aged ≥70 years with incurable stage III/ IV solid tumors or lymphoma initiating high-risk systemic therapy. Pretreatment cognitive screening was assessed using Mini-Cog. Outcomes included grade 3-5 non-hematologic toxicity, unplanned hospitalization, and early treatment discontinuation within 3 months, and all-cause mortality at 6 months and 1 year. Multivariable logistic and Cox models adjusted for sociodemographic, clinical, and geriatric variables. Results: Among 368 patients (mean age 77.2 years), 32% had abnormal cognitive screening. Abnormal screening was associated with higher odds of unplanned hospitalization (OR = 1.79, 95% CI, 1.04-3.10). Age modified this association, with stronger effects among patients aged 70-79 years (OR = 3.16, 95% CI, 1.57-6.46) but not ≥80 years (OR = 0.72, 95% CI, 0.25-1.99). Abnormal screening was also associated with increased mortality at 6 months (HR = 1.94, 95% CI, 1.24-3.03) and 1 year (HR = 1.61, 95% CI, 1.16-2.24), but not with toxicity or early discontinuation. Conclusions: Abnormal cognitive screening was associated with increased hospitalization and early mortality among older adults with advanced cancer receiving systemic therapy. Routine cognitive screening may improve risk stratification and treatment planning.

items.title: Toxicity, health-related quality of life and sexuality after molecular profile-based adjuvant treatment in high-intermediate risk endometrial cancer, PORTEC-4a
items.authors: Van den Heerik ASVM, Post CCB, Haverkort MAD, et al.
items.abstract: Background: PORTEC-4a was the first to incorporate molecular-integrated profile-guided adjuvant treatment in early-stage high-intermediate-risk endometrial cancer (EC), demonstrating non-inferiority. Here, adverse events (AE), health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and sexual health are reported. Methods: 564 patients were randomised to molecular-based adjuvant treatment (n = 367) or standard vaginal brachytherapy (VBT, n = 197). In the molecular-profile arm, patients underwent observation, VBT or pelvic radiotherapy according to molecular-integrated profile. HRQoL and sexual functioning were assessed with EORTC QLQ-C30 and EN24 modules and compared with age-matched normative data. Results: Median follow-up was 58.1 months; 523 (92.7%) patients were evaluable. Grade 1-2 AEs were less frequent in the molecular-profile arm at treatment completion compared with the standard arm (28.3% vs. 45.2%, p < 0.01), without differences in grade 3-4 AEs (p = 0.46). Throughout follow-up, treatment-related grade 3-4 AEs were rare (1% vs. 2%). HRQoL remained comparable to normative data over time. Sexual interest/activity was similar between arms, but lower than normative values. 75.5% of patients reported ≥1 reason for sexual inactivity; disease-related sexual inactivity decreased from 24.2% to 9.2% at 3 years. Conclusion: Molecular-guided adjuvant treatment for patients with high-intermediate riskEC is associated with low toxicity, preserved HRQoL and slightly reduced sexual activity due to personal factors (no partner, sex not important in their relationship or partner-related medical issues) rather than their own illness.

items.title: The Complementary Impact of Amino Acid PET with Diffusion and Perfusion MRI for Glioblastoma Tumor Delineation
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Younus E, Qian J, Johnson DR, et al.
items.abstract: Background: While standard MRI imaging is known to underestimate glioblastoma tumor extent, advanced imaging techniques including 18-FDOPA PET, dynamic contrast enhanced (DCE) perfusion MRI, and diffusion weighted MRI (DWI) have been utilized on clinical trials to identify tumor within and beyond gadolinium enhancement for radiation targeting. This clinical trial analysis quantifies how DCE, DWI and 18-FDOPA PET identify tumor beyond standard imaging, and whether these techniques are complementary and feasible. Methods: Patients with newly diagnosed glioblastoma enrolled on a phase II clinical trial underwent pre-radiation 18-FDOPA PET/CT, DCE, DWI, and standard MRI sequences. Tumor volumes were separately delineated using each imaging modality and incorporated into radiation target volumes, and were compared for overlapping and non-overlapping segments. Results: In 153 enrolled patients included in this analysis, tumor was identified beyond conventionally used radiation volume expansions of 5-, 10-, 15-, and 20 mm from standard MRI tumor volumes in 86%, 56%, 38% and 20% of patients, respectively. Advanced imaging techniques identified partially overlapping tumor volumes; PET identified tumor outside of the advanced MRI subvolumes in 88%, while DWI and DCE identified tumor outside of standard MRI and PET in 95% cases, indicating these imaging techniques are complementary. Conclusions: Advanced imaging techniques including DCE, DWI, and 18-FDOPA PET allow complementary delineation of glioblastoma beyond contrast-enhancing tumor from standard MRI, and may be most valuable when used in combination. These advanced imaging methods can potentially facilitate accurate tumor targeting with reduced CTV expansions to spare normal tissue and enable safe hypofractionated radiation therapy.

items.title: Particle therapy for T3N0M0 non-small cell lung cancer: a Japanese nationwide prospective registry study
items.authors: Nakamura M, Kubo N, Maruo K, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Particle therapy offers dosimetric advantages over conventional photon therapy, potentially minimizing toxicities for larger tumors. This study evaluated the clinical outcomes and safety of particle therapy for cT3N0M0 non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) using a Japanese nationwide prospective registry. Methods: This multicenter prospective observational registry study included patients with cT3N0M0 NSCLC who were treated with proton beam therapy or carbon-ion radiotherapy between May 2016 and June 2021. Overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), cumulative incidence of local failure (LF), and adverse events were evaluated. Prognostic factors were compared using the Cox proportional hazards model and the cumulative incidence curves were compared using the Fine-Gray model. Results: A total of 96 patients were evaluated. With a median follow-up of 53 months, the 3-year OS, PFS, and LF rates were 48.1 %, 33.0 %, and 19.2 %, respectively. Grade 3 or higher adverse events were observed in 5 patients (5.2 %), with no Grade 5 events reported. In multivariate analysis, concomitant interstitial lung disease and low vital capacity were identified as significant prognostic factors for both OS and PFS. No statistically significant associations with OS or PFS were detected for tumor size > 5 cm, treatment modality, or chemotherapy. Conclusion: Particle therapy showed encouraging survival outcomes and a low reported incidence of severe toxicity in patients with cT3N0M0 NSCLC, potentially offering a definitive treatment option for those who are medically inoperable or decline surgery.

items.title: Second Cancer Risk in Female Survivors of Hodgkin Lymphoma: A National Cohort Analysis Across Treatment Eras
items.authors: Macklin-Doherty A, Cunningham D, Chau I, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Subsequent primary malignancies (SPMs) are the leading cause of long-term treatment-related mortality in Hodgkin lymphoma (HL). Although treatments have evolved substantially over recent decades, few studies have demonstrated reductions in SPM risks following modern treatments, nor how such changes should inform survivorship care and screening. We analyzed SPM risks in a large female cohort of childhood and adult patients with HL treated over a 60-year period. Materials And Methods: This population-based cohort study included 7,428 women diagnosed with HL before age 36 years in England and Wales from 1954 to 2010, with follow-up through 2018. SPMs were ascertained via national cancer registry linkages. Standardized incidence ratios (SIRs), absolute excess risks, and multivariable models were used to assess temporal trends and associations with treatment. Results: During a median follow-up of 20.2 years, 1,200 women developed 1,467 invasive cancers (SIR, 3.3 [95% CI, 3.1 to 3.5]), most commonly breast, lung, and thyroid cancers. Solid tumor risks were the highest following radiotherapy, with a strong dose-dependent response. Alkylator use with radiotherapy was associated with reduced risks of breast cancer but increased risks of GI cancers. Solid cancer risks decreased by 25% between treatment periods 1954-1989 and 2000-2010. The decrease was attenuated and nonsignificant after adjustment for radiotherapy but not affected by adjustment for chemotherapy. No decline was observed for hematologic malignancies. Cumulative incidence of SPMs reached 36% at 50 years. Conclusion: Female patients treated in more recent eras have a substantially lower long-term risk of solid SPMs largely attributable to the reduced use, dose, and improvement in radiotherapy. Nevertheless, persistently elevated risks remained beyond 50 years of follow-up, particularly for lung and breast cancer, underscoring the need for lifelong surveillance and targeted screening of survivors.

items.title: Izalontamab Brengitecan in Recurrent or Metastatic Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma: The PANKU-Esophagus01 Randomized Clinical Trial
items.authors: Lu Z, Huang Z, Meng X, et al.
items.abstract: Importance: Effective therapy remains lacking for patients with advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) whose disease progressed after standard treatment. Izalontamab brengitecan, an epidermal growth factor receptor and human epidermal growth factor receptor 3 bispecific antibody-drug conjugate with a topoisomerase I inhibitor, Ed-04, has shown clinical activity in ESCC in a phase 1b study. Objective: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of izalontamab brengitecan compared with chemotherapy in patients with advanced ESCC who progressed after first-line programmed cell death 1 protein (PD-1)/programmed cell death 1 ligand 1 (PD-L1) inhibitor plus platinum-containing chemotherapy. Design, Setting, And Participants: This phase 3, open-label, randomized clinical trial was conducted across 80 hospitals in China. Patients with recurrent or metastatic ESCC that had progressed with first-line PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor plus platinum-containing chemotherapy were enrolled. Between March 19, 2024, and August 1, 2025 (final follow-up, October 17, 2025), a total of 704 patients were screened, and 497 were enrolled and randomized. Interventions: Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either izalontamab brengitecan (n = 249; 2.5 mg/kg on days 1 and 8 every 3 weeks) or physician-selected chemotherapy (n = 248; irinotecan, paclitaxel, or docetaxel) every 3 weeks. Main Outcomes And Measures: The dual primary end points were progression-free survival (PFS) assessed by blinded independent central review according to Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors version 1.1 and overall survival (OS). Results: Of 497 patients who underwent randomization (median age, 61.0 years [range, 34-76]; 448 male patients [90.1%]), 493 received study treatment. At this interim analysis, izalontamab brengitecan demonstrated statistically significant improvement in both PFS and OS. Median PFS by blinded independent central review was 4.17 months (95% CI, 3.61-4.53 months) with izalontamab brengitecan vs 1.97 months (95% CI, 1.61-2.73 months) with chemotherapy (hazard ratio, 0.50; 95% CI, 0.40-0.63; log-rank P < .001). Median OS was 9.79 months (95% CI, 7.89-11.01 months) with izalontamab brengitecan vs 7.20 months (95% CI, 6.18-7.82 months) with chemotherapy (hazard ratio, 0.63; 95% CI, 0.48-0.82; log-rank P < .001). items.title: Defining and managing NF1-related peripheral nerve sheath tumors at risk for malignant transformation: Consensus from the Atypical Neurofibroma Symposium
items.authors: Romo CG, Ahlawat S, Amrami KK, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract People with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) are at risk for developing peripheral nerve sheath tumors (PNSTs) ranging from benign neurofibromas to high-grade sarcomas. PNSTs known as atypical neurofibromas are at increased risk for malignant transformation. In 2017 the term ANNUBP (atypical neurofibromatous neoplasm of uncertain biologic potential) was proposed for PNSTs at increased risk for malignant transformation based on histopathologic features. Subsequently it was recognized that PNSTs not meeting ANNUBP criteria could still have concerning clinical, imaging and molecular features. A State of the Science conference addressed how to define these pre-cancerous PNSTs and reached consensus regarding clinical management and priority areas of research. Key recommendations from this symposium include: (1) using a combination of histologic, molecular and imaging features to define pre-malignant “at-risk” PNST; (2) recognizing that people with NF1 may be divided into “higher-risk” and “average-risk” for MPNST based on features such as their germline NF1 variant, internal tumor burden and history of malignancy or radiotherapy and; (3) the need to validate consensus screening and surveillance strategies based on personal and tumor-related risk factors. These recommendations will advance the ability to standardize care, and potentially fuel research that enables early diagnosis, prevention of malignant transformation and improved outcomes.

items.title: Safely Navigating the MR-Linac: A New Risk Framework for Prostate SBRT Patients with Cardiac Devices
items.authors: Cooney JD, Gambino H, Lee D, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Prostate stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) on a 1.5-T magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) linear accelerator (MR-linac) combines high-contrast intrafraction imaging with online adaptive replanning and enables focal dose intensification. Patients with cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIEDs) nonetheless face barriers to MR-guided radiotherapy (MRgRT), because existing guidance addresses diagnostic MRI and radiotherapy exposures separately and does not specify fraction-level requirements for their combination. We developed and implemented a framework integrating both domains in one operational pathway. Methods: A multidisciplinary group synthesized diagnostic MRI, radiotherapy, and MR-linac safety evidence into a dual-axis risk model. The MRI/CIED axis is keyed to device exposure (generator-lead configuration, manufacturer conditions, and sequence-level radiofrequency and gradient compliance) rather than anatomic field of view. The radiotherapy (RT)/CIED axis stratifies neutron production, cumulative generator dose, generator-to-field geometry, and pacing dependence. A failure mode and effects analysis translated high-priority scenarios into hold points and role assignments; the pathway is implemented prospectively for CIED patients on a 1.5-T MR-linac. Results: The two axes intersect in a matrix assigning every patient to one of six classes: LOW, LOW/INTERMEDIATE, INTERMEDIATE, INTERMEDIATE/HIGH, HIGH, or HOLD. Each class specifies monitoring, consent, interrogation, programming, personnel, and platform requirements. These are implemented through a day-of-treatment workflow with named role ownership and sequential hold points aligned with the 2026 American College of Radiology Manual on MR Safety. Two determinations override the matrix: MR-hold defers MRgRT irrespective of radiotherapy category, and RT-high defaults to computed tomography-guided radiotherapy. Conclusions: By unifying MRI- and radiotherapy-specific device risks, the dual-axis framework converts categorical CIED exclusion into a graded, prospectively assigned disposition and makes every decision auditable. It is in prospective clinical use and offers appropriately selected patients a conservative route to MRgRT and the documentation from which multi-institutional validation can be built.

items.title: Bioabsorbable spacer-assisted high-dose proton beam therapy for unresectable locally advanced pancreatic cancer of the body or tail: a feasibility and safety study
items.authors: Nakamura H, Nanno Y, Terashima K, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: Anatomical proximity to gastrointestinal (GI) organs can preclude dose-escalated irradiation for locally advanced pancreatic cancer (LAPC). We evaluated the safety and feasibility of bioabsorbable spacer-assisted high-dose proton beam therapy (PBT) for unresectable LAPC of the pancreatic body or tail. Materials And Methods: This exploratory retrospective analysis used retrospectively reviewed perioperative data and retrospectively or prospectively collected PBT data. Fourteen patients with presumed nonmetastatic LAPC underwent placement of a bioabsorbable polyglycolic acid (PGA) spacer. Thirteen received definitive PBT at 67.5 or 75 Gy (relative biological effectiveness [RBE]) in 25 fractions. The composite primary safety endpoint was the occurrence of a Clavien-Dindo grade ≥III surgical complication or a CTCAE grade ≥3 adverse event related to definitive PBT or concurrent chemotherapy. Results: Spacer placement achieved ≥10 mm tumor-GI separation in all 14 patients; 13 completed definitive PBT. No Clavien-Dindo grade ≥III surgical complication occurred. Four of 13 definitive-PBT patients (30.8%) experienced at least one qualifying safety event: one experienced grade 3 nausea and three other patients experienced grade 3 leukopenia/neutropenia. No grade ≥3 structural GI injury was observed. Median follow-up was 19.3 months. Median overall and progression-free survival were 24.8 and 11.8 months, respectively; 1- and 2-year local control rates were 81.5% and 38.2%. Conclusion: Bioabsorbable spacer-assisted high-dose PBT was technically feasible in this selected cohort. However, this small, uncontrolled study cannot establish a low risk of uncommon or late adverse events or support conclusions regarding comparative safety or efficacy.

items.title: A retrospective study on stereotactic radiotherapy or whole brain radiotherapy for brain metastases of small cell lung cancer
items.authors: Pan J, Qiang SJ, Wu C, et al.
items.abstract: Purposes: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) frequently results in brain metastases, which significantly impact survival rates. Although whole-brain radiotherapy (WBRT) is the conventional approach, it is associated with neurocognitive side effects. Stereotactic radiotherapy (SRT) offers accurate targeting but lacks established guidelines for managing SCLC's numerous metastases. This research conducted a comparative analysis of SRT, WBRT, and WBRT combined with a boost (WBRT+Boost) to inform clinical management strategies. Methods: A retrospective analysis was conducted involving 337 patients with SCLC who presented with brain metastases and were treated at Zhejiang Cancer Hospital between 2019 and 2026. The patient groups consisted of those receiving SRT (n = 95), WBRT alone (n = 181), and WBRT+Boost (n = 61). The primary endpoints of the study were intracranial progression-free survival (iPFS) and overall survival (OS). Statistical analyses employed Kaplan-Meier curves, log-rank tests, Cox proportional hazards models, and 1:1 propensity score matching (PSM) to control for confounding variables. Results: Pre-PSM, SRT demonstrated a longer median OS compared to WBRT alone (13.47 vs. 8.27 months, P = 0.013), although the differences in iPFS were not statistically significant. Following PSM, the differences in OS diminished (SRT vs. WBRT: 11.77 vs. 8.70 months, P = 0.412), while the WBRT+Boost significantly improved iPFS compared to SRT (8.17 vs. 5.87 months, P = 0.021). Multivariate analysis identified a Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS) of ≥ 90 (HR, 0.63; P = 0.006) and the presence of synchronous metastases (HR, 0.62; P = 0.013) as factors associated with improved OS. Conversely, the presence of extracranial metastases (HR, 2.24; P < 0.001) and more than three brain lesions (HR, 1.44; P = 0.045) were linked to worse OS. Additionally, immunotherapy administered after radiotherapy was found to be protective. Conclusion: Radiotherapy modality did not significantly impact OS, but WBRT+Boost may enhance intracranial control. Immunotherapy integration is critical. Future prospective studies should define optimal strategies and synergy with immunotherapy. Clinical Trial Number: Not applicable.

items.title: Low-Dose CT Lung-RADS 2022 for the Management of Screening- and Non-Screening-detected Lung Cancer Associated with Cystic Airspaces
items.authors: Mascalchi M, Cavigli E, Puliti D, et al.
items.abstract: Background Lung cancer associated with cystic airspaces (CA) can be misinterpreted as a benign lesion, leading to missed or delayed diagnosis; however, the effect of the Lung Imaging Reporting and Data System (Lung-RADS) 2022 criteria remains unverified. Purpose To retrospectively determine the frequency and outcomes of lung cancer associated with CA during screening and explore the potential effect of Lung-RADS 2022 on earlier diagnosis. Materials and Methods This secondary analysis included participants with lung cancers from three trials: the National Lung Screening Trial (2002-2007); Italian Lung Cancer Screening Trial, or ITALUNG (2004-2010); and German Lung Cancer Screening Intervention trial, or LUSI (2007-2016). Two radiologists jointly reviewed low-dose CT images to identify and morphologically characterize lung cancer associated with CA. Associations with histologic features, stage, and other variables were assessed. Lung cancer-specific survival was analyzed using Fine-Gray regression accounting for the competing risk of non-lung cancer death. Multivariable models were adjusted for age, sex, stage, detection status, and trial. Lung-RADS 2022 criteria for atypical pulmonary cysts were applied. Results Seventy-three cancers associated with CA were identified in 1258 participants (median age, 64 years [IQR, 61-69 years]; 43 male), including 44 of 716 (6.1%) screening-detected and 29 of 542 (5.4%) non-screening-detected cancers. Multilocular morphologic type was associated with a more advanced stage than unilocular morphologic type (12 of 24 vs 15 of 49; P = .02). The 5-year lung cancer-specific survival was 51.4% (95% CI: 39.3, 62.3) for cancers associated with CA and 53.2% (95% CI: 50.1, 56.2) for 1054 participants with noncystic non-small cell lung cancer. No evidence of a difference in survival was observed (subdistribution hazard ratio, 1.15 [95% CI: 0.81, 1.63]; P = .44), and results remained consistent in multivariable models. Lung-RADS 2022 might have enabled earlier diagnosis in 55 of 73 cancers associated with CA (75%). Conclusion Lung cancer associated with CA accounted for 6.1% of screening-detected and 5.4% of non-screening-detected lung cancers. Outcomes were similar to those of noncystic non-small cell lung cancer, and Lung-RADS 2022 may facilitate earlier diagnosis. Clinical trial registration nos. NCT00047385, NCT02777996, and ISRCTN N30604390 © RSNA, 2026 Supplemental material is available for this article. See also the editorial by Byrne and Hammer in this issue.

items.title: T cell redirection in high-risk smouldering multiple myeloma: can deep responses prevent progression to multiple myeloma?
items.authors: María-Victoria Mateos
items.abstract: Nature Reviews Clinical Oncology, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41571-026-01230-2 The randomized phase II ImmunoPRISM trial has shown encouraging efficacy of the B cell maturation antigen-targeted bispecific T cell engager teclistamab in high-risk smouldering multiple myeloma, although several aspects constrain interpretation of the results. Herein, I discuss aspects that should be addressed in future research, such as patient selection, treatment duration, clinically relevant end points and adequate treatment in the control arm, to establish whether deep responses translate into durable prevention of progression with an acceptable benefit–risk profile.

items.title: Intismeran Autogene plus Pembrolizumab for Resected Stage IIB to IV Melanoma
items.authors: Long GV, Khattak MA, Gogas HJ, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Intismeran autogene (intismeran) is an individualized neoantigen therapy that is designed to induce new T-cell responses and expand preexisting T-cell responses against patient-specific tumor neoantigens, which may potentially improve the efficacy of adjuvant therapy in patients with melanoma. Methods: In this phase 3, double-blind trial, we randomly assigned patients with completely resected stage IIB to IV cutaneous melanoma in a 2:1 ratio to receive intramuscular intismeran (at a dose of 1 mg) or placebo every 3 weeks for nine doses; all the patients received intravenous pembrolizumab (at a dose of 400 mg) every 6 weeks for nine cycles. The primary end point was investigator-determined recurrence-free survival, assessed in a time-to-event analysis. Key secondary end points included investigator-determined distant-metastasis-free survival (assessed in a time-to-event analysis) and safety. Results: A total of 1137 patients underwent randomization: 757 to the intismeran-pembrolizumab group and 380 to the placebo-pembrolizumab group. The median follow-up was 24.6 months. Recurrence-free survival at 24 months was 82.2% in the intismeran-pembrolizumab group and 70.0% in the placebo-pembrolizumab group (two-sided P<0.001); the piecewise hazard ratio was 0.99 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.66 to 1.49) before 6 months and 0.42 (95% CI, 0.30 to 0.58) after 6 months. Distant-metastasis-free survival at 24 months was 88.5% with intismeran-pembrolizumab and 80.2% with placebo-pembrolizumab (two-sided P = 0.002); the piecewise hazard ratio was 1.01 (95% CI, 0.58 to 1.79) before 6 months and 0.50 (95% CI, 0.34 to 0.73) after 6 months. Adverse events of grade 3 or higher occurred in 23.6% of the patients in the intismeran-pembrolizumab group and 20.3% of the patients in the placebo-pembrolizumab group. Eight patients (1.1%) in the intismeran-pembrolizumab group died from an adverse event; five of the deaths occurred before intismeran was administered. Conclusions: Adjuvant therapy with intismeran plus pembrolizumab significantly prolonged recurrence-free survival and distant-metastasis-free survival as compared with pembrolizumab alone in patients with completely resected, high-risk cutaneous melanoma. (Funded by Merck Sharp and Dohme and Moderna; ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05933577.).

items.title: Unsupervised deep learning model for fast energy layer pre-selection of delivery-efficient proton arc therapy plan optimization of nasopharyngeal carcinoma
items.authors: Yang B, Lian H, Liu G, et al.
items.abstract: Proton arc therapy (PAT) is an emerging and promising modality in radiotherapy, offering improved dose distribution and treatment robustness over conventional intensity-modulated proton therapy. Yet, identifying the optimal energy layer (EL) sequence remains challenging due to the high computational demand and prolonged treatment delivery time. This study proposes unsupervised deep learning for fast EL pre-selection, targeting EL switching (ELS) time and plan quality.Approach. We introduce a spot-count representation that combines structure-specific spot counts with spatial dose-influence features, organized by gantry angle and EL. A U-Net-style model, SPArc_dldp, uses this representation and water-equivalent thickness features to score candidate ELs, with training objectives based on spot counts and ELS time. We evaluated SPArc_dldp against SPArc_pso in 35 paired nasopharyngeal carcinoma cases, including nine-scenario robust optimization and evaluation.Main results. SPArc_dldp achieved a significantly higher nominal clinical target volume (CTV) conformity index (CI: 0.613±0.034 versus 0.557±0.040; p<0.001). It showed better homogeneity (HI: 0.395±0.048 versus 0.414±0.060; p=0.135). EL-selection computation took 2.218±0.022 ms for DL and 14.18±2.71 s for PSO. DL had significantly shorter ELS time (28.59±4.01 versus 72.19±5.56 s; p<0.001), but higher optic-nerve and parotid mean doses. Following robust optimization, DL had a higher CTV root-mean-square deviation dose-volume histogram area (RVH-AUC: 10.71±1.00 versus 8.69±0.73 per-fraction Gy(RBE)·%; p<0.001), indicating greater dose variation.Significance. The proposed spot-count representation supports rapid EL pre-selection for PAT planning. In this exploratory comparison, SPArc_dldp achieved higher nominal CI and shorter ELS time, alongside higher mean doses to some OARs and greater CTV dose variation.

items.title: Global Authorship Patterns in Phase III Solid-Tumor Trials Presented at the ASCO Annual Meeting, 2015-2025
items.authors: Sarfraz A, Hodgson LC, Abraham SM, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Authorship of phase III oncology trials reflects broader patterns of scientific leadership, including access to resources, research infrastructure, and global participation. However, how these factors intersect with gender over time remains incompletely characterized. We evaluated trends in authorship across phase III solid-tumor trials presented at the ASCO Annual Meeting from 2015 to 2025. Methods: We conducted a repeated cross-sectional study of phase III solid-tumor abstracts presented at ASCO (2015-2025). Author gender was assigned using a multistep approach based on publicly available data. Outcomes included authorship by role (first v senior), tumor track, funding source, trial-origin geographic region, and trial-origin World Bank income group. Multivariable logistic regression identified factors associated with female authorship. Results: Among 1,517 abstracts (3,034 authorships), 27.9% of authors were women. Female authorship increased from 24.9% in 2015-2020 to 30.0% in 2021-2025 (P = .002). Women were more likely to be first than senior authors (54.7% v 45.3%, P = .002) and were less likely to hold senior authorship overall (adjusted odds ratio [OR], 0.76, 95% CI 0.65-0.90; P = .001). Temporal gains were driven by increased female senior authorship (OR, 1.55 [95% CI, 1.20 to 1.99]; P = .001). Female authorship was lower in several tumor types and in East Asia and Pacific versus North America (OR, 0.65 [95% CI, 0.48 to 0.87]; P = .003). Funding and income group were not associated with female authorship. Conclusion: Women remain underrepresented in phase III oncology trial authorship, particularly in senior roles and across certain tumor types and regions, suggesting persistent gaps in authorship representation that may reflect broader structural barriers.

items.abstract: Recent randomized trials have demonstrated clinical benefits of proton craniospinal irradiation (pCSI) in patients with leptomeningeal disease. However, limited availability of proton therapy restricts its widespread implementation. In contrast, photon CSI (xCSI) is more accessible but results in higher radiation doses to organs at risk (OAR)—most notably the bone marrow. This discrepancy raises critical questions regarding treatment-related toxicity and whether the oncological benefit observed with pCSI can be effectively reproduced using modern photon radiotherapy techniques.

items.title: Aligning Clinical Trial Reporting: A systematic analysis and position statement by the International Consortium for MDS
items.authors: Brunner AM, Getz TM, Pugh K, et al.
items.abstract: Variability in how clinical trial elements are reported can hinder accurate interpretation and comparison of trial results. Here, we systematically analyzed published manuscripts of therapeutic clinical trials in myelodysplastic syndromes/neoplasms (MDS) focusing on how key data elements were reported and made recommendations on how to improve this reporting. We included peer-reviewed full text manuscripts that reported results of clinical trials in MDS and were published between January 1, 2015 to December 31, 2024. We analyzed the presence or absence of several pre-determined key reporting elements and then synthesized these data to evaluate for consistency across manuscripts. We identified substantial variability in descriptions of patient characteristics, as well as the definitions used for response criteria. For example, baseline ANC was reported in only 16% of lower-risk MDS studies and 23% of higher-risk MDS studies, while baseline bone marrow blast percentage was reported in only 55% of higher-risk MDS manuscripts. In addition, response endpoints lacked standardization, with six unique definitions of RBC transfusion independence identified in lower-risk MDS trials and seven different definitions of overall response rate identified in higher-risk MDS trials. Informed by the results of this analysis, we then performed a modified-Delphi process for members of the International Consortium for MDS (icMDS) to develop consensus-based recommendations for consistent and accurate reporting of MDS clinical trial results. We advocate that these recommendations serve as benchmarks and templates for clinical trial reporting in MDS to improve interpretability and comparison of results.

items.title: PREDICT: a clinical tool to decide when to include the pelvis in prostate cancer radiotherapy. Development and multicohort external validation
items.authors: Rosich A, Cuervo B, Ferrer J, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Decisions regarding elective pelvic irradiation in prostate cancer are often informed by the Roach formula, which uses only prostate-specific antigen (PSA) and Gleason score. We developed PREDICT to estimate individualized pretreatment dissemination risk from routine variables, evaluated nodal prediction externally and secondarily explored its implications for pelvic irradiation selection. Methods And Materials: PREDICT was developed in 73 203 SEER patients diagnosed in 2018-2022, using age, PSA, Gleason pattern, biopsy cores and clinical stage, with nodal risk standardized to a 15-node dissection. Four predictor-specific versions fitted in SEER were applied without external refitting or imputation to four surgical cohorts (1923 patients; 106 node-positive). With pathologic nodal status as the reference, we estimated the threshold matching the sensitivity of the POP-RT criterion (Roach risk of 20% or more). Results: In 17 164 operated patients, the area under the curve (AUC) for nodal involvement was 0.793 with PREDICT versus 0.749 with Roach (paired difference, +0.043; 95% CI, +0.035 to +0.052), without a significant difference from MSKCC/Kattan. Externally, the paired difference versus Roach was -0.006 (-0.046 to +0.035). Observed nodal involvement increased from 1.6% to 25.1% across PREDICT risk bands in SEER and from 1.8% to 27.9% externally. In SEER, 15.3% (95% CI, 14.4% to 16.2%) matched POP-RT-criterion sensitivity with 7.0 fewer pelvic fields per 100 patients. This reduction was not demonstrated externally, and no common threshold was validated across populations. Conclusions: PREDICT provides individualized pretreatment risk estimates to inform discussion of pelvic irradiation alongside clinical judgment. About 15% is a candidate threshold derived in SEER; threshold transportability and benefit from PREDICT-guided irradiation require prospective validation.

items.title: Cross-ancestry proteome-wide mendelian randomization of plasma proteins and breast cancer susceptibility
items.authors: Wu X, Godbole D, Williams J, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Background The plasma proteome may help connect inherited breast cancer susceptibility to biologically interpretable and potentially actionable pathways, but proteome-wide evidence across ancestries remains limited. Methods We conducted proteome-wide Mendelian randomization (MR) analyses of breast cancer risk using cis -protein quantitative trait loci for 1,962 distinct plasma proteins from 34,557 European-ancestry participants in the UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project. Breast cancer genome-wide association studies included 156,901 cases and 204,634 controls of European, East Asian, and African ancestries. Ancestry-specific MR estimates were combined by fixed-effects meta-analysis. Candidate proteins were further evaluated through subtype-specific and reverse-direction MR analyses, statistical colocalization, replication in independent European and East Asian proteomic datasets, and analyses of associations between protein polygenic scores and breast cancer status in All of Us. Results Twelve proteins achieved Bonferroni significance in the cross-ancestry meta-analysis ( P < 0.05/1,971 tests), including eight previously reported proteins and four newly prioritized by MR. DNPH1 showed cross-ancestry heterogeneity, while CASP8, RALB, and USP28 showed cross-subtype heterogeneity after accounting for shared controls (all P < 0.05/12). Complementary support varied: six candidates showed strong colocalization (PPH4 ≥ 0.80); four replicated with a consistent direction and nominal significance in deCODE, two in the Japan COVID-19 Task Force, and four in All of Us (all P < 0.05). The strongest cumulative support was observed for LRRC25, PARK7, and LRRC37A2. Conclusions These findings prioritize circulating protein candidates for mechanistic, prevention-oriented, and translational follow-up in breast cancer, while underscoring the need for larger ancestrally diverse proteomic resources to support equitable target and biomarker discovery.

items.title: Independent validation of a predictive risk model for contrast-enhancing brain lesions supports enhanced periventricular radiosensitivity and variable proton RBE
items.authors: Bauer J, Adena-Eichkorn T, Velkova L, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: Contrast-enhancing brain lesions (CEBLs) were reported as MR-imaging (MRI) endpoint to assess dose effects in healthy brain tissue following proton radiotherapy (PRT) of low-grade-glioma (LGG) patients. A voxel-level risk model was proposed with absorbed dose (D), dose-averaged linear energy transfer (LETD), and proximity to the ventricular system as risk factors. We validated this model in an independent LGG patient cohort. Material And Methods: LGG patients treated at the same institution but more recently (2015-2019) were considered. For each patient, follow-up MRI data were screened for CEBLs, complication-risk maps were calculated and patient-level NTCPCEBL values were determined according to the original model. Eventually, risk model coefficients were updated by regressing the original logistic model to the validation cohort (validC) data. Results: The validC comprised 112 subjects. Observed CEBL incidence of 21% was the same as in the modelling cohort (modelC); observed number of CEBLs and median lesion volume were considerably smaller in the validC, (NvalidC = 26, NmodelC = 67 and Vmed,validC = 110 mm3, Vmed,modelC = 235 mm3). Good calibration of the original patient-level NTCPCEBL model was obtained in the validC. Update of the model coefficients yielded a more pronounced LETD-effect and a 2.4 times higher odds ratio for the complication risk in the periventricular space (PVS). Conclusions: The presented validation confirms an enhanced radiosensitivity of the PVS, a variable proton RBE, and supports serial complication characteristics of the brain. This underlines the need for a PRT strategy that actively spares the PVS under consideration of an LETD-dependent proton RBE. Clinical Trial Information: The study was approved by the ethics committee of the Heidelberg University Hospital (ethics vote: S-516/2022).

items.title: A novel deep learning segmentation and multimodal radiomics approach for radiation proctitis prediction in cervical cancer
items.authors: He C, Wang Z, Liu Z, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to develop and validate a novel interpretable framework integrating a deep segmentation network with multimodal radiomics to improve the prediction performance of radiation proctitis (RP) in cervical cancer patients undergoing radiotherapy. Methods: This retrospective study included 650 cervical cancer patients, who were divided into training and internal device test sets, and independent device test set, based on different computed tomography (CT) scanners. A Mamba-enhanced deep learning network was constructed to enhance global modeling capability in pelvic anatomical structures, providing reliable regions of interest segmentation for radiomics and adaptive radiotherapy. In multimodal radiomics approach, foundation model features were integrated with radiomics and clinical data to mitigate inherent bias in training data, thereby enhancing the prediction of RP. Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) technology was employed to explain the contributions of multimodal features to the prediction performance. Results: The segmentation model achieved dice similarity coefficients (DSC) of 90.76% and 85.33% on the internal and independent device test sets, outperforming existing models. Ablation study confirmed the contribution of each module to segmentation performance. The multimodal radiomics model demonstrated robust performance in predicting RP, with area under the curve (AUC) values of 0.882 and 0.865 on the internal and independent device test sets, surpassing single-feature models. Additionally, SHAP analysis revealed the interactions between key features, including dosimetric and foundation model features, which contributed to improve decision interpretability. Conclusion: This study significantly improved the robustness and accuracy of RP prediction by integrating the deep segmentation model and multimodal radiomics, providing a promising clinical applications framework for individualized radiotherapy planning. Clinical Trial Number: Not applicable.

items.title: Evolution of bubble dynamics in viscoelastic tissue during boiling histotripsy: A numerical and ex vivo experimental study
items.authors: Wu M, Zhang C, Ma X, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Background The viscoelastic properties of soft tissue and liquefied debris can influence bubble dynamics during boiling histotripsy (BH), while quantitative assessment of cavitation evolution is desirable for treatment monitoring. Purpose To investigate the effects of tissue viscoelasticity and liquefaction progression on cavitation dynamics during BH and to evaluate inertial cavitation dose (ICD) as a quantitative indicator of tissue fractionation. Methods A modified Keller–Miksis equation coupled with a linear Voigt model was used to simulate a gas bubble within a liquid‐filled cavity surrounded by viscoelastic tissue while varying acoustic power and cavity radius. Passive cavitation detection (PCD) was performed in ex vivo bovine liver (n = 20) and human breast fibroadenoma (BFA) treatment groups (n = 18). Lesion area and ICD were quantified in bovine liver, whereas B‐mode sonography and histology were used to assess BFA tissue changes. Longitudinal bovine‐liver data were analyzed using repeated‐measures one‐way ANOVA with Geisser–Greenhouse correction and prespecified paired comparisons with Holm–Bonferroni adjustment. Paired t‐tests or Wilcoxon matched‐pairs signed‐rank tests were used as appropriate. Effect sizes were reported as partial eta squared (ηp2${{\eta }_p}^2$), Cohen's dz${{d}_z}$, or rank‐biserial correlation (rrb${{r}_{rb}}$). Spearman's rank correlation was used to assess the association between lesion area and ICD. Results Numerical simulations demonstrated that radial stress induced by bubble oscillation at the liquid–tissue interface contributes to mechanical disintegration, with interfacial stresses gradually decreasing as tissue liquefaction progresses. The PCD monitoring approach enables determination of the onset and evolution of bubble cavitation characteristics. In ex vivo bovine liver, treatment cycle had significant overall effects on lesion area [F (2.805, 53.29) = 68.42, P < 0.0001, ηp2${{\eta }_p}^2$ = 0.783] and ICD [F (2.044, 38.84) = 109.6, P < 0.0001, ηp2${{\eta }_p}^2$ = 0.852]. items.title: Patterns of Treatment and Clinical Outcomes in Patients With Stage 1/2 EGFR-mutated Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Treated With Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy: A Global, Multicenter, Retrospective Study
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Lin SH, Okishio K, Mizutani H, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: We report clinical outcomes, mutation testing patterns, and treatment patterns from a global, real-world, retrospective, observational study in patients with stage 1/2 epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Methods And Materials: Data were extracted from medical records of adults with stage 1/2 EGFR-mutated NSCLC (diagnosed January 2016-December 2019), who underwent stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) as standard of care. The primary objective was assessment of real-world progression-free survival (rwPFS). Secondary objectives included assessment of mutation testing patterns, treatment sequencing post-SBRT, real-world time to next treatment or death (rwTTNTD), and real-world overall survival (rwOS). Results: Data were extracted from medical records of 82 patients across six countries; 66% of patients had medically inoperable tumors; 43% had tumors harboring exon 19 deletion (Ex19del), 55% had L858R, 1% had both Ex19del and L858R, and 1% had L858R and an exon 20 insertion. Overall, 91% of patients had stage 1A/1B disease and 9% had stage 2A/2B. All patients underwent SBRT as standard of care; 31 patients (38%) progressed following SBRT. Of patients who received subsequent treatment (n = 25), most received EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs; 88%; n = 22/25); first-/second-generation EGFR-TKIs n=17, third-generation EGFR-TKIs n=5. Median (95% confidence interval [CI]) rwPFS, rwTTNTD, and rwOS were 47.1 (38.7-57.8), 49.8 (40.7-not estimable [NE]), and 62.9 (50.8-NE) months, respectively. The rwPFS rates at 12, 24, 36, 48, and 60 months (95% CI) were 90% (81-95), 76% (65-84), 65% (53-74), 48% (35-60), and 34% (19-48), respectively. Conclusions: In this global, real-world, retrospective study in patients with stage 1/2 EGFR-mutated NSCLC who underwent SBRT, the majority of whom had medically inoperable tumors, the 4-year rwPFS rate was <50%. Further studies are needed to confirm the potential role for EGFR-TKI therapy in this setting.

items.title: Self-Reported Dysphagia in Head and Neck Cancer Survivors From Diagnosis to Twelve Months Post Treatment and Predictors for Moderate to Severe Long-Term Dysphagia
items.authors: Johansson-Malmeling C, Petersson K, Finizia C, et al.
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Dysphagia is a common complication of head and neck cancer (HNC) and its treatment. This study examined swallowing‐related quality of life from diagnosis to 12 months after treatment, compared swallowing outcomes across tumor sites and treatment modalities, and identified predictors of moderate‐to‐severe dysphagia. Methods The M. D. Anderson Dysphagia Inventory (MDADI) was completed by 445 patients receiving curatively intended HNC treatment pre‐treatment and at 3‐, 6‐, and 12‐months post‐treatment. Results Swallowing‐related quality of life worsened during treatment, the poorest scores at 3 months post‐treatment; 21.6% reported moderate‐to‐severe dysphagia, decreasing to 12.5% at 12 months. Risk factors for dysphagia at 12 months included stage IV disease, surgery combined with (chemo)radiotherapy, smoking cessation within 12 months, and pre‐treatment sick leave. Patients with cervical carcinoma of unknown primary (CCUP) had the poorest outcomes. Conclusions Swallowing function declined during treatment. Patients receiving surgery combined with (chemo)radiotherapy and patients with CCUP are at increased risk of long‐term dysphagia and require closer follow‐up.

items.title: A prospective comparative evaluation of dysphagia in surgically resected oral cavity cancers treated by dysphagia optimized volumetric modulated arc therapy (DO-VMAT) versus standard volumetric modulated arc therapy (S-VMAT): DECODE trial
items.authors: Mondal P, Nanda SS, Mukherji A, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Radiotherapy induced dysphagia is a common side effect in post-operative oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma (OCSCC) patients, affecting quality of life (QOL). Dysphagia-optimized radiotherapy reduces dose to dysphagia aspiration-related structures (DARS) while maintaining oncological efficacy. This prospective study compared dysphagia outcomes between DO-VMAT and S-VMAT in resected oral cavity cancers. Materials And Methods: This was a two-arm comparative, prospective, interventional study conducted between June 2022 and December 2023 with 50 patients of OCSCC on adjuvant chemoradiation divided in 1:1 ratio to either arm. Acute and chronic toxicities were graded by RTOG criteria. Dysphagia assessment by physician-reported toxicity, 100 ml water swallow test (WST), fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES-DIGEST), and patient-reported QOL using MD Anderson Dysphagia Inventory (MDADI) were performed. Kaplan-Meier method was used to analyze disease-free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS). Results: DO-VMAT achieved significantly lower mean doses to DARS (superior constrictor p = 0.023, middle constrictor p = 0.003, inferior constrictor p = 0.001) compared with S-VMAT. Acute dysphagia rates were comparable (p = 0.238), chronic effects including dysphagia (p = 0.041) and feeding tube dependency (p = 0.041) were significantly lower with DO-VMAT. At 12 months, objective swallowing outcomes favored DO-VMAT, with lower FEES-DIGEST scores (p = 0.018) and higher MDADI composite scores (p = 0.03). 2-year OS (82% vs 78%) and DFS (74% vs 76%) were comparable between S-VMAT and DO-VMAT. Conclusion: DO-VMAT is safe and feasible for adjuvant radiotherapy in OCSCC. It significantly reduces late dysphagia and improves patient-reported QOL without affecting disease control or survival.

items.title: Dose-dense neoadjuvant bi-weekly nab-paclitaxel followed by epirubicin-cyclophosphamide versus bi-weekly docetaxel followed by epirubicin-cyclophosphamide in patients with HR+/HER2- early breast cancer: a multicentre, randomised, phase III trial
items.authors: Zhang M, Qin Y, Wan J, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Dose-dense adjuvant chemotherapy prolongs survival in breast cancer and has been translated into neoadjuvant settings. Although weekly nanoparticle albumin-bound (nab)-paclitaxel yields superior pathological complete response (pCR) rates relative to solvent-based paclitaxel, data supporting its incorporation into a dose-dense neoadjuvant regimen-particularly for hormone receptor positive/human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 negative (HR+/HER2-) tumours-remain limited. This trial therefore evaluated whether a bi-weekly dose-dense nab-paclitaxel schedule improves the proportion of residual cancer burden (RCB) 0/Ⅰ compared with a comparable dose-dense docetaxel regimen, each followed by dose-dense epirubicin plus cyclophosphamide. Methods: This was a multicentre, randomised, phase III trial done at three hospitals in China. HR⁺/HER2⁻ patients (cT1-3/N0-1/M0) were randomised 1:1 using dynamic allocation with Pocock minimisation on Ki-67 and TNM stage. The experimental arm received nab-paclitaxel 260 mg/m² intravenously on day 1 every two weeks for four cycles; the control arm received docetaxel 100 mg/m² on the identical schedule. Both cohorts subsequently received epirubicin 90 mg/m² plus cyclophosphamide 600 mg/m² intravenously on day 1 every two weeks for four cycles. Primary endpoints were RCB 0/Ⅰ rate; secondary endpoints encompassed disease free survival (DFS), overall survival (OS), and safety. Results: Between December 2019 and December 2020, 388 patients (194 per arm) were enrolled. The nab-paclitaxel arm attained an RCB 0/Ⅰ rate of 20.1% (95% CI 14.41-26.72), significantly exceeding the docetaxel arm's 11.34% (95% CI 6.92-15.81; χ²=5.62, P = 0.018). pCR was achieved in 15.98% (95% CI 10.81-21.16) of the nab-paclitaxel group versus 10.31% (95% CI 6.01-14.60) of the docetaxel group (χ²=2.73, P = 0.098). Multivariate analysis confirmed a statistically significant favourable impact of nab-paclitaxel on RCB 0/Ⅰ. Five-year DFS was comparable (90.21% vs. 87.11%; HR: 1.14, 95% CI 0.64-2.05; P = 0.656), as was five-year OS (96.34% vs. 95.31%; HR: 0.64, 95% CI 0.29-1.42; P = 0.274), indicating no significant survival disparity. Grade 3/4 adverse event incidence was similar (30% vs. 38%). The most frequent all-grade toxicities (neutropenia, nausea, myalgia) occurred at comparable rates; however, grade 3/4 peripheral sensory neuropathy was observed exclusively in the nab-paclitaxel cohort. No treatment-related mortality was reported.…

items.title: A Rising Tide: Trends & Predictors of Resident Research Productivity in Canadian Radiation Oncology
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Kotrri E, Petrushkevich A, Warner A, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Research is an integral component of Canadian radiation oncology (RO) residency training. Reports suggest increasing RO resident publication rates, but national trends remain underexplored. This study examined residency research productivity and predictors over a 25-year period. Methods: A database was compiled including graduating residents from Canadian RO residency programs between 1998 and 2023. Demographic information was extracted from public sources. PubMed-indexed publications during medical school and residency were identified and categorized by journal, research type, authorship position and impact factor (IF). Graduates were divided into six temporal cohorts. Linear and chi-square trend tests analyzed rates over time. Univariable and multivariable regression analyses identified authorship predictors. Results: Among 416 graduates (43% female), 970 residency publications were identified (52% first-author). Retrospective studies were most common (29%). The proportion of publishing residents increased from 29.1% (1998-2002) to 80.8% (2020-2023) (p < 0.001). Mean ± SD any-author publications increased from 0.5 ± 1.0 to 4.9 ± 5.0 across cohorts, and first-author from 0.3 ± 0.9 to 2.5 ± 2.7 (p < 0.05). Publications in journals with IF > 4 increased significantly over time. Later graduation cohorts, larger programs, and two specific residency programs predicted higher resident research output (p < 0.05), whereas gender did not. Medical school research productivity correlated positively with residency output. Conclusions: Canadian RO resident research productivity has increased markedly over 25-years, with predictors including more recent graduation cohorts, larger program size and training program. These findings establish a contemporary benchmark for Canadian RO research productivity.

items.title: Risovalisib for PIK3CA-mutated recurrent or persistent ovarian clear cell carcinoma: a single-arm, multicentre, phase 2 trial
items.authors: Li J, Yonemori K, Niimi K, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Ovarian clear cell carcinoma is a rare but aggressive and biologically distinct subtype of ovarian cancer, in which PIK3CA mutations are common. Advanced ovarian clear cell carcinoma is very difficult to treat, and after failure of platinum-based chemotherapy, therapeutic options are limited. We aimed to evaluate the anti-tumour activity and safety of the PI3Kα inhibitor, risovalisib, for treatment of patients with recurrent or persistent PIK3CA-mutated ovarian clear cell carcinoma. Methods: We conducted a single-arm, phase 2 trial of the PI3Kα inhibitor, risovalisib, in 27 centres in China and 12 centres in Japan. Eligible participants were adult patients (aged 18 years or older, with an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 or 1) with recurrent or persistent PIK3CA-mutated ovarian clear cell carcinoma and one to three lines of previous systemic anti-tumour treatment. Risovalisib was given orally at 40 mg daily in 21-day cycles until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, or other protocol-defined reasons for discontinuation. The primary endpoint was objective response rate assessed by blinded independent review committee (BIRC) using Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumours (version 1.1), among all treated patients with a confirmed PIK3CA hotspot mutation and baseline tumour assessments with measurable lesions per BIRC (efficacy analysis set). The primary endpoint was considered met if the lower 95% CI was greater than 8%. Safety analyses were performed in all patients who received at least one dose of risovalisib (safety analysis set). The trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05043922) and is ongoing but no longer recruiting patients. Findings: Between Oct 6, 2021, and Jan 31, 2024, 93 patients were enrolled and received risovalisib. The median age was 49 years (IQR 43-58), all patients were female, 52 (56%) were from Japan, 41 (44%) were from China, and 63 (68%) had two or more previous lines of therapy. The median duration of follow-up was 14·5 months (IQR 8·6-18·3). The objective response rate was 29 (35% [95% CI 25-46]) of 84 patients in the efficacy analysis set. The most commonly reported grade 3 or worse treatment-related adverse events in 93 patients were rash (30 [32%]), hyperglycaemia (28 [30%]), and decreased weight (7 [8%]). Treatment-related serious adverse events occurred in 36 (39%) patients, the most common being rash (eight [9%]), pneumonitis (six [6%]), and decreased appetite (four [4%]). There were no treatment-related deaths.…

items.title: Dynamic Range Modulation via Integrated Universal Range Shifter and Ridge Filter: Enabling Simplified Delivery for FLASH-Enabled IMPT
items.authors: Wang H, Quan H, Pang B, et al.
items.abstract: In proton FLASH therapy, using a transmission beam with hypofractionated doses can minimize energy layer switching interruptions to preserve FLASH effect. However, intensity-modulated proton therapy (IMPT) struggles to achieve high FLASH dose rates. This study proposes a novel system that combines universal range shifters (URS) and universal ridge filters (URF) to enable FLASH effect in IMPT.Approach: Water equivalent thickness (WET) optimization was first performed to determine the URS thickness relative to tumor depth, followed by URF modulation to broaden the monoenergetic Bragg peak for longitudinal target coverage. Plan optimization incorporated a spot sparsification algorithm. The proposed system using 218 MeV beams was evaluated in three anatomical sites (brain, liver, and lung tumors) for 10 cases each. Furthermore, this study evaluated the impact of hardware switching speeds and two delivery strategies: (1) bi-URS, constraining URS transitions to binary states, and (2) bi-URF, restricting URF modulation to binary configurations.Main Results: The bi-URS and TB plans achieved mean D98% of 98.30% ± 0.80% versus 98.60% ± 0.90% in brain cases, and 98.40% ± 0.50% versus 97.20% ± 1.00% in liver cases, respectively. Compared to bi-URF, the bi-URS modality significantly reduced delivery time (e.g., brain: 0.305 ± 0.09 s vs. 1.031 ± 0.096 s, p < 0.001). And it demonstrated superior target conformity index (CI) (brain: 0.660 ± 0.020 and liver: 0.653 ± 0.022) compared to TB plans (brain: 0.357 ± 0.082, p < 0.001 and liver: 0.479 ± 0.100, p = 0.012) while maintaining high FLASH average dose rate (ADR) coverage (V40Gy/s of 87.60 ± 15.96% for brain and 91.21 ± 14.42% for liver cases) with URF 20-ms switching speed. Furthermore, it effectively spared the Dmax of hippocampus (bi-URS: 19.00 ± 5.80 Gy, TB: 37.71 ± 17.71 Gy, p=0.041) in brain cases and the residual liver V5 Gy in liver cases (bi-URS: 27.79 ± 10.9%, TB: 68.64 ± 18.72% , p=0.002). However, in lung cases, the CI of the bi-URS modality, while superior to that of the TB modality, remained below the clinical expectation of 0.6.Significance: The combined URS and URF delivery strategy (bi-URS) improved dose conformity of the target, and maintained high FLASH effect coverage in brain and liver cases, demonstrating its potential as a Bragg-peak PBS approach for FLASH radiotherapy.&#xD.

items.title: National cancer database analysis of uterine carcinosarcoma: An updated series in locally advanced stage patients
items.authors: Zitter R, Sivananthan AP, Son CH, et al.
items.abstract: Objective: Uterine carcinosarcoma is a rare, aggressive malignancy with high rates of distant failure, and the optimal sequencing of adjuvant chemotherapy and radiation in locally advanced disease is undefined. We evaluated whether the sequencing of adjuvant therapies is associated with overall survival (OS) in surgically managed FIGO stage III-IVA uterine carcinosarcoma. Methods: We identified 4593 patients with surgically treated FIGO stage III-IVA uterine carcinosarcoma in the National Cancer Database (2004-2020). Patients were categorized as chemotherapy only (CO), radiation only (RO), sequential chemoradiation (SCRT), concurrent chemoradiation (CRT), or no adjuvant therapy. CRT was defined as chemotherapy and radiation start dates within 14 days, with SCRT separated by more than 14 days. OS was estimated by Kaplan-Meier and compared using Cox regression, with inverse probability of treatment weighting, propensity-score matching, and landmark analyses as sensitivity analyses. Results: SCRT had the highest 2-year OS (67.3%) versus CO (51.4%), CRT (52.8%), and RO (34.6%). On MVA, SCRT was associated with improved OS versus CO (adjusted HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.60-0.82; univariable HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.61-0.74), whereas CRT was not (HR 1.12, 95% CI 0.80-1.57). SCRT benefit persisted across weighted, matched, and landmark analyses and after exclusion of stage IVA patients (HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.59-0.80). Age and lymphovascular space invasion were independently prognostic. Conclusions: In locally advanced uterine carcinosarcoma, SCRT was associated with superior OS compared with CO, while CRT was not. These data support prospective evaluation of adjuvant treatment sequencing in this histology.

items.title: International Cross-Age Consensus Guideline on Measurable Residual Disease Assessment in Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia
items.authors: Kotrova M, Alten J, Biondi A, et al.
items.abstract: Measurable residual disease (MRD) assessment is central to risk stratification, response evaluation, and relapse detection in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). However, substantial global variability in its methodology and implementation persists. Differences in sampling strategies, detection methods, reporting thresholds, and interpretation criteria hinder cross-trial comparability and clinical standardization. To address this, an international expert panel representing major pediatric and adult study groups and reference laboratories developed consensus recommendations, using a structured current-practices survey followed by a multi-round Delphi process. Consensus was achieved on 38 of 41 statements. Recommendations span three domains: pre-analytical requirements, technical and nomenclature standards, and MRD-based remission and relapse definitions. Bone marrow was endorsed as the reference specimen for MRD assessment, and MRD was prioritized over cytomorphology in cases of discordance. Principles for risk- and actionability-guided late MRD monitoring, confirmation of MRD reappearance, and MRD-informed relapse assessment were also defined. Among the key technical consensus statements, a standardized MRD assay nomenclature was adopted. Areas without consensus-namely, anticoagulant choice for PCR-based MRD, interpretation of isolated BCR::ABL1 reconversion, and the exclusive use of MRD to define remission-highlight ongoing biological and clinical complexity. This guideline, applicable across all ages, provides a practical framework to standardize MRD assessment in ALL and support MRD-guided clinical decision-making.

items.title: Dose-time-response relationships between radiation dose to the circulating blood and temporal changes in peripheral blood biomarkers during chemoradiation of non-small cell lung cancer
items.journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
items.authors: Gaudreault M, Johnstone P, Chen A, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Chemoradiotherapy commonly causes radiation-induced lymphopenia, neutropenia, and anemia, as measured by reductions in absolute lymphocyte count (ALC), absolute neutrophil count (ANC), and hemoglobin level (Hb). We aimed to quantify these hematological toxicities and characterize dose-time-response relationships between temporal changes in peripheral blood biomarkers and radiation exposure to the circulating blood during volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT) definitive chemoradiotherapy for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Methods And Materials: Blood biomarker measurements were collected from 93 NSCLC patients, treated between 2018 and 2024, at pre-, during-, and post-treatment time points. Radiotherapy prescription doses were 60 Gy in 30 fractions, 55 Gy in 20 fractions, or 50 Gy in 25 fractions with concurrent platinum-based chemotherapy. Organs at risks were delineated by the TotalSegmentator software. The blood dose-volume histogram was estimated through simulations of blood dynamics using the HEDOS software and VMAT dose accumulation was calculated with the BeamSplitter algorithm. Dose-time-response relationships were modelled by linear and exponentially decaying curves, from which rates of change were extracted and goodness of fit quantified using the R2- value. Results: Baseline blood biomarker values (median ± interquartile range) were (1.8±0.9) × 109/L for ALC, (5.6±3.0) × 109/L for ANC, and 132±19 g/L for Hb. Prior to treatment, 0%, 0%, and 30% of patients exhibited lymphopenia, neutropenia, and anemia, respectively. During treatment, these proportions increased to 71%, 19%, and 77%. Dose-response analysis revealed rates of change at low doses of radiation: -69%/Gy (ALC), -83%/Gy (ANC), and -3%/Gy (Hb), with model fits showing R² values between 0.78 and 0.96. Conclusions: Hematological toxicities were frequent in NSCLC patients treated with VMAT chemoradiotherapy. Radiation exposure was associated with changes in circulating lymphocyte counts and hemoglobin, supporting prospective investigation into reducing circulating blood dose during chemoradiation to mitigate hematological toxicity.

items.title: Variation in baseline estrogen levels, menopause-related adverse events and early study discontinuation among women on the placebo-controlled MAP.3 exemestane prevention trial
items.authors: Ho V, Pasquet R, Singh RJ, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Breast cancer prevention has been demonstrated using aromatase inhibitors (AIs) including exemestane, but menopause-related adverse events can limit adherence. We hypothesized that estrogens are potential biomarkers that could be measured at baseline to predict the probability of AI-related adverse events. Patients And Methods: Estrone (E1) and estradiol (E2) levels were measured from Mammary Prevention 3 trial baseline serum samples (n = 4111) using liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry. Hot flashes, fatigue, and joint pain were assessed using the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events v4.0. Severe toxicity (grade ≥3) and moderate toxicity (grade ≥2) were contrasted with less severe toxicity. Logistic regression was used to estimate odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs) for each symptom (years 1 and 5) and baseline E1 and E2 levels. Results: Women on exemestane with the highest levels of E1 or E2 at baseline were significantly more likely to develop severe hot flashes (E1: ORyr-1 = 3.8, 95% CI 1.6-10.5) and (E2: ORyr-1 = 4.2, 95% CI 1.6-13.1) compared with women in the lowest quartile, with a clear dose-response observed at year 1. Severe joint pain was associated with higher baseline E1 and E2 levels in women on exemestane at year 1 but was only statistically significant for E1 (quartiles 2 and 3). There were no significant associations in the placebo group. Women in the highest quartile of E1 or E2 were significantly more likely to discontinue protocol therapy within the first 12 months, independent of assigned treatment, compared with women in the lowest quartile. Conclusions: Postmenopausal women with elevated estrogen levels who initiate exemestane are at greater risk for the development of severe hot flashes and joint pain and may benefit from measures to limit early discontinuation.

items.title: Effect of two common GVHD prophylaxis regimens on the gut microbiome in a randomized phase 3 trial
items.authors: Wirbel J, Saber W, Martens MJ, et al.
items.abstract: Allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation can cure certain hematological disorders but has many complications. In retrospective studies, low gut microbiome diversity is associated with adverse clinical outcomes. In 2023, the Blood and Marrow Transplant Clinical Trials Network 1703 randomized phase 3 trial demonstrated the superiority of post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) and mycophenolate mofetil to tacrolimus and methotrexate (Tac/MTX) for graft-versus-host disease prophylaxis in participants with hematological malignancies undergoing allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation. Here we report on the microbiome-focused companion study to 1703, Blood and Marrow Transplant Clinical Trials Network 1801, which coenrolled participants and shared trial registration. The primary endpoint was association between microbiome diversity at neutrophil engraftment and non-relapse mortality after 1 year; secondary endpoints included associations with other clinical outcomes and with baseline microbiome diversity. Based on 2575 longitudinally collected stool samples from 304 participants (Tac/MTX n = 147, PTCy n = 157), no association between engraftment microbiome diversity and non-relapse mortality was observed (P = 0.314), not meeting the primary endpoint. Lower baseline microbiome diversity was associated with shorter overall survival (P = 0.007). Safety data were reported in the original 1703 publication. In exploratory analyses, microbiome diversity and absolute microbial load were lower in PTCy compared to Tac/MTX on days 14-28 following HCT, independent of non-prophylaxis antibiotics exposure. Microbial domination events, when a single species exceeds 30% relative abundance, did not differ significantly between study arms and reflected both pathogen blooms and less severe disruptions of the microbial community. Clostridium scindens and secondary bile-acid metabolism pathways were less prevalent in PTCy than in Tac/MTX following HCT. In summary, we find prophylaxis regimens likely exert independent effects on both the microbiome and immune compartments and can also impact their interaction. Understanding whether and how microbiome-targeted interventions might improve transplant outcomes will therefore require careful disentangling of these effects within each specific treatment context. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03959241 .

items.title: MGMT Protein Expression and Promoter Methylation in Glioblastoma Survival: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.authors: van Heumen M, Schmelzer V, Panayotopoulos L, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Background Glioblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in adults. Methylation of the O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase ( MGMT ) promoter is the only clinically used biomarker predicting response to alkylating agents such as temozolomide and is associated with improved survival. However, its predictive accuracy is limited by an intermediate gray zone and variability in assessment methods. To reduce overtreatment of patients, improved stratification strategies are needed, potentially through integration of additional biomarkers such as MGMT protein expression. Methods We performed a systematic review to evaluate studies comparing the prognostic value for progression-free survival and overall survival of MGMT promoter methylation and MGMT protein expression in glioblastoma patients treated with temozolomide, including 33 independent cohorts with a total of 4,691 patients. We searched three databases up to May 2025. Risk of bias was assessed with a modified Quips tool. Results and discussion Methylation-specific PCR and pyrosequencing indicated stronger prognostic value than immunohistochemical assessment of MGMT protein expression with hazard ratios (HRs) of 2.07 (95%CI 1.61–2.66), 2.13 (95%CI 1.64–2.75), and 1.50 (95%CI 1.26–1.79), respectively. An inverse correlation between MGMT promoter methylation and protein expression was observed in only 52% of assessed studies, suggesting that promoter methylation and protein expression may contribute independently to prognosis. Conclusion Substantial variability in methylation assays and protein cut-offs underscores the need for methodological harmonization in future studies and clinical practice. Integration of MGMT protein expression with promoter methylation refines identification of primary temozolomide-resistant tumors and supports the debate of withholding temozolomide in patients unlikely to benefit.

items.title: Making patient-reported outcomes reusable at scale
items.authors: Boyer L, Leucht S, Fernandes S, et al.
items.abstract: Patient-reported outcomes (PROs) are essential to understanding how people live with illness, treatment, and care, and are increasingly promoted for routine use in clinical practice, quality improvement, and value-based health care. PROs are also increasingly relevant in digital health and artificial intelligence applications, both as inputs to predictive models and as outputs reflecting patient-centred aspects of health. Yet, PROs remain difficult to reuse at scale: their implementation is inconsistent across health-care settings, measurement approaches are highly heterogeneous, and PROs are rarely available as large, standardised, analysable datasets suitable for multisite analyses and advanced analytics, including artificial intelligence models.

items.title: Home-Built environment as medicine for long-term cancer survivorship: a hard pill to prescribe
items.journal: JNCI: Journal of the National Cancer Institute Advance Access
items.abstract: Abstract Cancer survivorship is increasingly recognized as a chronic, accelerated aging–related state of health, with long-term care occurring largely within the community and home-built environment (H-BE)–the human-made or modified structures of the dwelling. Lifelong environmental exposures–such as fine particulate matter, circadian-disrupting light, and toxic chemicals–can exacerbate post-treatment inflammaging, disrupt resolution of inflammation, and shape trajectories of long-term outcomes. Yet patient-level H-BE interventions targeting these modifiable, non-lifestyle risk factors remain an overlooked clinical domain in survivorship research, clinical guidelines, and care delivery.In this Commentary, we present an evidence-based, living framework that positions the H-BE as an emerging, prescribable target for mitigating late toxicities, symptom burden, and their physiological precursors in aging cancer survivors. The framework is structured across eight Emerging Frontline Domains, interdependent capability areas to guide next-generation survivorship trials in the practice of H-BE as medicine and advance clinical translation primary care–level H-BE screening and dual clinical–environmental risk stratification; referral pathways and follow-up structures with BE health expertise; real-world characterization of H-BE exposure scenarios; drug–environment interaction mapping; shared mechanistic and biomarker-informed domains capturing inflammatory burden, inflammaging, and capacity to resolve inflammation; implementation technologies enabling longitudinal remote monitoring; and decentralized, adaptive and personalized trial designs to support scalable outpatient delivery.H-BE as medicine addresses a critical gap for middle-aged and older cancer survivors–those most affected by treatment-driven inflammaging, multimorbidity, and prolonged home exposure–and offers a mechanistically robust, actionable roadmap to advance H-BE interventions from research through feasibility testing into survivorship clinical practice.

items.title: Mid-trial dosimetric analysis of the korean radiation oncology group 19 - 09 multi-institutional prospective cohort study on breast cancer
items.authors: Lee W, Kim YJ, Kim TH, et al.
items.abstract: Background: The Korean Radiation Oncology Group 19 - 09 multi-institutional clinical trial investigates the effect of regional nodal irradiation (RNI) omission on regional recurrence rates after neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by breast-conserving surgery, and sentinel lymph node biopsy in cT1-3N1 and ypN0 breast cancer patients. This mid-trial analysis evaluates dosimetric deviations among enrolled patients using an artificial intelligence (AI) auto-contouring engine. Methods: We analyzed dose-volume histograms of 366 patients enrolled from eight institutions based on an AI auto-contoured reference structure set. Of these, 176 received whole breast and regional nodal irradiation (WBI + RNI), while 190 received whole breast irradiation only (WBI). Results: Dosimetric outliers were observed in both groups. In the WBI + RNI group, 25 (14%) and 30 (17%) patients were outliers in D95% of axillary levels II and III, respectively. The corresponding counts in the WBI group were 17 (9%) and 16 (8%), respectively. Especially, 7 (58%) of 12 patients treated by one physician in the WBI + RNI group were outliers for axillary level III. Similarly, among the 49 patients treated by another physician in the WBI + RNI group, 21 (43%) were outliers for axillary level II and 21 (43%) for level III. Regarding the breast CTV, all outlier patients except one were treated by the two physicians. Conclusion: Significant dose deviations were observed, indicating that comparing the WBI + RNI and WBI groups alone may inadequately assess the clinical impact of RNI omission. Therefore, the final analysis will evaluate the association between specific regional nodal doses and clinical outcomes.
