items.title: Pre-selection of breast cancer patients for deep inspiration breath-hold proton radiotherapy: Who benefits?
items.journal: Tech Innov Patient Support Radiat Oncol
items.authors: Visser F, Boersma LJ, Kneepkens E, et al.
items.abstract: Aim: Intensity modulated proton therapy (IMPT) in breath-hold (BH) could reduce the mean heart dose (MHD) compared to IMPT in free breathing (FB) in a subgroup of breast cancer (BC) patients. The aim of this study is to identify subgroups of BC patients who benefit the most from IMPT in BH. Methods: We conducted an in-silico study involving fifteen left-sided BC patients treated with regional nodal irradiation, including the internal mammary lymph nodes. IMPT plans were created on FB and BH-CT planning scans. Based on the MHD and mean lung dose (MLD), the difference in risk (ΔNTCP) of acute coronary events (ACE) and secondary lung cancer (SLC) between IMPT BH and FB-plans was calculated for subgroups based on the Dutch national indication protocol for IMPT. A Wilcoxon signed-rank test (p = 0.05) identified subgroups for whom the absolute ACE-risk with IMPT BH was ≥1% lower than with IMPT FB. Results: All ACE ΔNTCP values favoured IMPT in BH over FB (p ≤ 0.002). Age- and risk-stratified analysis showed that in patients ≤ 60 years and with cardiac risk factors, the difference in NTCP between proton-BH and FB was ≥1%. In 14 of 15 plans, BH increased MLD (p < 0.05), yielding higher SLC risks in smokers ≤ 50 years. Median (25th-75th interquartile range) MLD was 6.7 (5.4-7.5) Gy for BH vs 5.4 (4.1-6.6) Gy for FB. Conclusions: Female patients ≤60 years, with left-sided BC, IMN indication and cardiac risk factors benefit most from IMPT in BH. For smokers ≤ 50 years, an individualized FB versus BH comparison is required due to the potential increase in secondary lung cancer risk associated with higher MLD.

items.title: Bias-corrected respiratory motion standard deviation from amplitude-binned 4D-MRI for radiotherapy planning
items.authors: Ferraro M, Tadimalla S, Navarro Salazar F, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Background Respiratory‐resolved magnetic resonance imaging (4D‐MRI) provides superior soft‐tissue contrast for characterizing respiratory motion in radiotherapy, but its geometric fidelity depends on the reconstruction and binning strategy. As with 4D‐CT, peak‐to‐peak amplitude derived from binned 4D‐MRI is prone to underestimation. However, as acquisitions span many respiratory cycles, the standard deviation (SD) of motion, required for probability‐based planning approaches such as mid‐ventilation, may be estimated accurately, provided binning‐induced bias is corrected. Purpose To develop and validate a motion SD estimator for equal‐probability amplitude‐binned 4D‐MRI data that corrects for systematic underestimation caused by intra‐bin motion variability. Methods 4D‐MRI data were acquired on a dynamic motion phantom driven by five patient‐derived respiratory traces. Images were reconstructed using both a standard non‐uniform fast Fourier transform (NUFFT) and the compressed sensing‐based XD‐GRASP algorithm with varying numbers (2–20) of equal‐probability respiratory amplitude bins. An SD estimator based on the law of total variance was implemented to correct for intra‐bin variance. The accuracy of peak‐to‐peak amplitude and SD was evaluated against ground‐truth physical phantom motion, with performance under deformable motion tested on a digital phantom (CoMBAT). Results Both reconstruction methods underestimated true peak‐to‐peak motion. While the inter‐bin SD calculation also underestimated motion variability, the proposed correction substantially mitigated this bias. It yielded robust SD estimates with median residual underestimation of 0.13 mm (5 bins) and 0.11 mm (10 bins) across patient traces. In CoMBAT, the absolute bias of the total SD estimate was below 3% from five bins onward. Conclusions The proposed estimator provides an accurate measurement of respiratory motion SD from amplitude‐binned 4D‐MRI by accounting for intra‐bin variability. This supports the reliability of 4D‐MRI for planning strategies dependent on motion probability distributions. Additionally, the confirmed underestimation of peak‐to‐peak amplitude highlights a fundamental limitation in defining internal target volumes directly from binned 4D‐MRI.

items.title: Comparison of dose escalation strategies for head and neck cancer patients using a radiobiological model of reoxygenation
items.authors: Guerrero M, Smith EC, Carlson DJ
items.abstract: Abstract Purpose Advanced imaging techniques for head‐and‐neck (HN) cancers can now quantify inter‐ and intra‐tumor variation in tumor hypoxia. Dose‐escalation based on pre‐treatment hypoxia in clinical trials typically boost initial hypoxic areas. However, longitudinal studies demonstrated that the location of hypoxic cells changes throughout treatment. Our goal is to further a model of reoxygenation and quantify the potential loss of biological effectiveness due to changes in hypoxia during treatment in dose‐escalation studies based on initial hypoxia only and compare this strategy to one based on patient selection according to imaging at weeks 0 and 2 of treatment and boosting of the whole treatment volume. Methods A published reoxygenation model based on LQ survival formulas with reoxygenation parameter Δ$\Delta$ is extended to allow for dose‐escalation with dose per fraction dH$d_H$ for initial hypoxic cells. The new model allows for hypoxic cells to miss the escalated dose depending on parameter “m” (m = 0 no hypoxic cells missed). Using published radiobiological parameters, we calculate the EQD2 when hypoxia is present for 70Gy delivered in 35 fractions with dH=2.2−2.6Gy$d_H=2.2-2.6{\rm Gy}$ using two different dose escalation strategies. Results Based on assumed parameters, the increase in EQD2 associated with escalated dose per fraction up to 2.6Gy cannot sufficiently compensate for the reduction in biological effect due to hypoxia if Δ=0$\Delta =0$. As Δ$\Delta$ increases to 0.2 and above the EQD2 becomes comparable to the non‐hypoxic values. Based on previous results, the dose‐escalation of the whole tumor after 20Gy based on hypoxia imaging at 2 weeks yields comparable or higher EQD2 values for more modest escalated doses to the whole tumor. Conclusions The proposed reoxygenation model allows evaluation and comparison of strategies for dose‐escalation to compensate for hypoxia during treatment and quantification of the limitations of dose‐escalation based on the initial distribution of hypoxia in a dynamic system of tumor oxygenation.

items.title: Monte Carlo (TOPAS) characterization of a proton therapy OBI: Automated source parameter optimization and analysis of CBCT acquisition dynamics
items.authors: Tan WC, Lee KH, Fu K, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Background The cumulative radiation burden from daily cone‐beam CT (CBCT) imaging is a significant concern. While Monte Carlo (MC) simulation provides the gold standard for patient‐specific dosimetry, clinical implementation is hindered by the complexity of characterising proprietary X‐ray source parameters. Furthermore, the dosimetric properties of the Hitachi ProBeat on‐board imager (OBI), which utilizes a fixed frame rate (FFR) acquisition logic, remains uncharacterized in the literature. Purpose To develop and validate a robust indirect characterization methodology that automates MC beam tuning using standard QA measurements, and to utilize this model to quantify the dosimetric impact of the Hitachi OBI's acquisition dynamics. Methods A TOPAS (Tool for Particle Simulation) MC model of the OBI was constructed through indirect characterization. An automated derivative‐free optimization framework was developed to tune source parameters (spectrum, filtration, focal spot) by minimizing the loss against 90 static projection measurements acquired on a standard CT dose index (CTDI) phantom. A global scaling factor was used to scale simulated dose to physical dose. The model was validated against radiophotoluminescent dosimeter (RPLD) measurements in an ATOM 701 adult male anthropomorphic phantom for head and thorax protocols. Finally, the validated model was used to isolate the dosimetric overhead introduced by the system's fixed frame rate (FFR) logic compared to a theoretical fixed angular interval (FAI) acquisition. Results Optimization of beam parameters through indirect characterization successfully converged, yielding a set of simulation parameters and a general scaling factor function. In the anthropomorphic validation, the model predicted central organ doses with a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 3.4%, with all in‐field validation points falling within ±$\pm$10% of physical measurements. Analysis of the gantry acquisition kinematics identified up to 9.4% additional projections that were not utilized during reconstruction, and up to 23.6% additional projections compared to a theoretical FAI acquisition. Simulations indicate dose hotspots approximately 10 mGy in bone structures due to kinematic oversampling at during acceleration/deceleration phases in FFR compared to FAI acquisition. Conclusions A high‐fidelity Monte Carlo beam model can be successfully derived solely from standard CTDI measurements via automated indirect characterization, achieving a 3.4% MAPE in anthropomorphic phantom validation.…

items.title: Reirradiation for Recurrent Craniopharyngioma-Long-Term Follow-up
items.authors: Hassan SP, Moreno AS, Mansour I, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: To report long-term tumor control, toxicity, and functional outcomes after a second course of fractionated radiation therapy for recurrent craniopharyngioma previously treated with radiation therapy. Methods And Materials: We identified all patients with craniopharyngioma with recurrent or progressive disease, unsuitable for further medical management or re-resection, who underwent 2 courses of fractionated photon radiation therapy at a single institution between 1998 and 2024. Reirradiation was delivered to 54 Gy in 30 fractions with full overlap of the initial target; dose constraints to optic nerves, chiasm, and brainstem were Dmax/D0.03cc (Maximum Dose or Dose to 0.03 cubic centimetres) ≤54 Gy. Outcomes were summarized descriptively. Results: Six patients received reirradiation a mean of 9.8 years (range, 5.6-20.5) after initial radiation therapy (50-54 Gy in 25-30 fractions). Median follow-up after reirradiation was 4.1 years (range, 0.4-8.8). At the last follow-up, 4 patients were alive, all with local disease control (2 with radiological regression, 2 with stable disease). Two deaths occurred (1 due to progressive disease and 1 due to functional decline with stable imaging). Visual outcomes were heterogeneous: 1 patient maintained intact vision; others had intermittent diplopia, bitemporal hemianopsia, or unilateral blindness with contralateral impairment. Endocrinopathy was frequent: 3 of 4 survivors had pan-hypopituitarism; 1 had partial deficits (hypothyroidism/amenorrhea). Functional status was impaired in survivors, with the inability to work or study due to fatigue, visual loss, or cognitive issues. Additional toxicities included posttreatment seizures requiring hospitalization (n = 1) and transient dexamethasone for headache (n = 1). Conclusions: In carefully selected patients lacking other curative options, modern highly conformal reirradiation can achieve meaningful local control after prior high-dose radiation therapy, but carries an additive risk of visual, endocrine, and functional morbidity. Decisions should be individualized within a multidisciplinary team to identify appropriate cases for reirradiation and to ensure thorough long-term follow-up to manage delayed toxicity.

items.title: Modeling Long-Term Progression-Free Survival in Newly Diagnosed Multiple Myeloma Treated With Daratumumab, Bortezomib, Lenalidomide, and Dexamethasone
items.authors: Sonneveld P, Zweegman S, Facon T, et al.
items.abstract: Daratumumab, bortezomib, lenalidomide, and dexamethasone (DVRd) significantly improved progression-free survival (PFS) versus VRd in newly diagnosed multiple myeloma (NDMM) in transplant eligible (TE; PERSEUS) and transplant-ineligible (TIE; CEPHEUS) populations. Median PFS with DVRd has not been reached in either study. This analysis extrapolated PFS data from PERSEUS and CEPHEUS (TIE subgroup) to estimate long-term outcomes for DVRd. Following UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidance on survival data extrapolation, seven parametric distributions were fitted to model PFS data. In PERSEUS (TE population), the projected median PFS range across distributions was 158-255 months versus 76-119 months and best-fit (exponential distribution) PFS estimates were 205 months (17.1 [range, 13.2-21.2] years, DVRd) versus 87 months (7.3 [range, 6.3-9.9] years, VRd). For CEPHEUS (TIE population), projected median PFS range across distributions was 96-118 months versus 52-54 months and best-fit estimates were 100 months (8.3 [range, 8.0-9.8] years, DVRd) versus 53 months (4.4 [range, 4.3-4.5] years, VRd). PFS projections were significantly longer with DVRd than VRd in TE (additional 118 months; 9.8 years) and TIE patients (additional 47 months; 3.9 years) across all seven distributions. These extrapolations reinforce the benefit of DVRd as standard of care in NDMM regardless of transplant eligibility.

items.title: Prognostic value of pre-treatment nodal appearance, volume and kinetics in High-Risk non-HPV related oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma
items.authors: Li GJ, Bin Johari MH, Hindle D, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: We investigated the risk and prognostic value of pre-treatment nodal progression to inform the safe de-escalation of elective nodal irradiation (ENI) in high-risk oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC). Methods: We identified patients with p16-negative, clinical T4, node-positive OPSCC treated consecutively with definitive radiotherapy between 2008 and 2021 from a prospectively maintained database. Pre-treatment diagnostic scans were compared against simulation scans to evaluate nodal disease based on pre-specified criteria, growth kinetics, and imaging-detected extranodal extension (iENE). Association of nodal factors and oncologic outcomes were assessed using regression models. Results: A total of 79 patients with a median 30-day interval between diagnostic and simulation scan were identified. Nodal growth was minimal with a median absolute change of + 0.5 cc and growth rate of 0.3%/day. Nodal kinetics and duration between imaging were not prognostic for treatment response. While no patients developed de novo pathological nodal disease, 14% of patients had indeterminant nodes on diagnostic scan, with 27% of these becoming pathological at time of simulation. Total nodal volume was highly correlated with presence of iENE, and was prognostic for locoregional failure (HR = 1.02, p = 0.03), distant failure (HR = 1.02, p = 0.02), and progression-free survival (HR = 1.02, p = 0.05). All regional failures were in-field of high dose treatment volumes. Conclusions: Pre-treatment nodal disease volume, but not growth kinetics, was a prognostic factor in locally advanced OPSCC. While lack of new nodal disease and minimal growth over a 30-day pre-treatment interval supports the investigation of novel timing of ENI, particular care should be taken in patients to identify and appropriately manage indeterminate nodes at risk for progression.

items.title: Barriers to treatment for patients diagnosed with cervical cancer: A systematic review
items.authors: Cortez CA, Taffe BD, Ellis C, et al.
items.abstract: Objective: Previous reviews have described disparities in the treatment of patients diagnosed with gynecologic cancers; however, these reviews are not systematic in nature, and none have focused specifically on individuals diagnosed with cervical cancer, who disproportionately represent marginalized populations in the US. This systematic review synthesizes evidence on treatment-related outcomes and multilevel determinants of care among US patients with cervical cancer. Methods: The protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42023413020). We searched PubMed, Scopus, and CINAHL for studies published through May 2026. Eligible studies examined treatment related outcomes among patients diagnosed with cervical cancer in the US. We identified 25 articles that met our inclusion criteria. Treatment-related outcomes were categorized and determinants (i.e., explanatory variables) were mapped on to the socioecological model. Results: Across 25 studies, 26 treatment-related outcomes were identified. Receipt of surgery, chemotherapy, and brachytherapy were the most frequently assessed outcomes. Key patient-level determinants included race/ethnicity, age, comorbidities, insurance, rurality, and distance to care. Minoritized populations, particularly Black, Hispanic, Native American, Pacific Islander, often experienced worse treatment outcomes. Older age was also a frequent barrier to treatment. Distance to care was inconsistently associated with treatment outcomes. Clinic-level determinants, such as care outside of large-volume facilities and academic medical centers, and contextual determinants, such as residing in a county with lower levels of income and education, were associated with worse treatment outcomes. Conclusions: Cervical cancer treatment in the United States is driven by multilevel determinants at the patient-, clinic-, and community-level. Addressing barriers to treatment requires attention to the broader structural and modifiable factors that hinder treatment for marginalized cervical cancer patients in vulnerable communities. Future studies should more rigorously and thoughtfully measure community-level and individual-level variables.

items.title: Pertuzumab in HER2-positive breast cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.authors: Aboushawareb H, Mohamed AW, Alghzawi HM, et al.
items.abstract: Background: HER2-positive breast cancer is a distinct subtype associated with less favorable outcomes without targeted therapy. Dual HER2 blockade with pertuzumab and trastuzumab has shown improved efficacy compared to single-agent approaches, but results across studies remain variable. This meta-analysis aims to evaluate the overall efficacy and safety of pertuzumab-based regimens. Methods: A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library was conducted to identify relevant RCTs. The quality of trials was assessed using the ROB-2 tool, and the certainty of the evidence was assessed using the GRADE tool. Data were synthesized using R. Results: This study included 8 RCTs with 8367 patients. Pertuzumab-based regimens were associated with improved overall survival. In the locally advanced or metastatic setting, a pronounced benefit was observed (HR = 0.71, 95% CI 0.65-0.77). However, in the neoadjuvant or adjuvant setting, the pooled hazard ratio (HR = 0.81, 95% CI 0.22-3.04), which was not significant. Progression-free survival (HR 0.74; 95% CI 0.67-0.83) was improved compared with the control group. In terms of safety, there was no significant difference in the incidence of any adverse events (risk ratio (RR) = 1.01; 95% CI 0.99-1.02) or grade ≥ 3 adverse events (RR 0.99; 95% CI 0.86-1.13) between the experimental and control groups. Conclusion: Pertuzumab-based dual HER2 blockade is associated with significant improvements in overall survival and progression-free survival in patients with metastatic HER2-positive breast cancer. Importantly, these survival benefits are not accompanied by a significant increase in overall or severe adverse events, supporting its favorable efficacy-safety profile across clinical settings.

items.title: Blood-based RNA biomarker for the early detection of ovarian cancer
items.authors: Wilhelm J, Kumar A, Vasiyani H, et al.
items.abstract: Flower-Win/Lose signaling underlies a tumor-host fitness conflict in ovarian cancer, in which tumor-derived exosomal Tu-stroma reduces the fitness of surrounding host cells, favoring tumor expansion within host tissues. High-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC), the most prevalent histotype of epithelial ovarian cancer and leading cause of ovarian-cancer-related mortality, arises from serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC), a noninvasive precursor typically identifiable only by histopathologic examination of excised fallopian tube tissue. Here we evaluated Tu-stroma, a tumor-associated long noncoding RNA enriched in serum extracellular vesicles (EVs), as a circulating biomarker in STIC and early-stage HGSC, representing the earliest histopathologically defined phases of disease. Tu-stroma was quantified in serum EVs from 506 individuals with histologically normal adnexa, benign-adnexal lesions, isolated STIC and HGSC across International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) stages I-IV. Normalized EV Tu-stroma ΔCT values were elevated in STIC (n = 43) and HGSC (n = 232) versus controls (n = 143) and benign-adnexal lesions (n = 88), including premenopausal women (controls = 57, benign = 34, STIC = 32, HGSC = 88). In paired receiver operating characteristic analyses, Tu-stroma showed higher discrimination than cancer antigen 125 (CA125) for STIC versus controls (area under the curve (AUC) = 0.99 versus 0.59, P < 0.001) and benign-adnexal masses (0.99 versus 0.31, P < 0.001), and for HGSC versus controls (AUC = 0.99 versus 0.96, P = 0.001) and benign-adnexal masses (0.98 versus 0.84, P < 0.001). Tu-stroma showed no systematic elevation across inflammatory or physiologic comparators (n = 116) or nonovarian malignancies (n = 160), each assessed against healthy controls (n = 100), supporting disease-context specificity. Modeled risk-enriched contexts yielded predictive values compatible with intended-use populations. These findings identify Tu-stroma as a candidate EV-RNA marker associated with pre-invasive and early HGSC biology. Prospective evaluation in consecutively enrolled real-world cohorts is required to validate diagnostic performance, predictive value and clinical utility.

items.title: Adjuvant Hepatic Arterial Infusion Pump Chemotherapy Without Systemic Therapy After Repeat Local Treatment for Patients With Liver-only Recurrence of Colorectal Cancer
items.authors: Outmani L, Filipe WF, Buisman FE, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Approximately 30% of patients develop liver-confined recurrences after local treatment for colorectal liver metastases (CRLM), which may be reduced by adjuvant therapy. Hepatic arterial infusion pump (HAIP) chemotherapy delivers high-dose liver-directed chemotherapy. Objective: To investigate adjuvant HAIP chemotherapy without systemic therapy in patients with resectable liver-confined recurrence after prior local treatment of CRLM. Methods: This multicenter, single-arm phase II trial enrolled patients with resectable recurrent CRLM across 3 centers in the Netherlands. Patients with prior or present extrahepatic disease were excluded. Adjuvant HAIP with floxuridine was administered up to 6 cycles. The primary endpoint was hepatic disease-free survival (hDFS) estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method, with a prespecified efficacy boundary of 36 months. Results: Forty-five patients underwent local treatment followed by adjuvant HAIP chemotherapy without systemic therapy. Twenty-eight patients(62%) were treated for a first recurrent CRLM, and 17 patients for a second or higher. Twenty-five patients (56%) had ≥3 CRLM. All patients started HAIP chemotherapy, with a median of 6 cycles (interquartile range: 4 to 6). After a median follow-up of 38.7 months (95% CI: 33.0-42.3), the median hDFS was 16.5 months (95% CI: 9.1-25.8). The median progression-free survival was 14.0 months (95% CI: 7.7-23.0), and the 3-year overall survival was 71% (95% CI: 58%-87%). Initial recurrence included the liver in 23 patients (51%). HAIP implantation-related complications (Clavien-Dindo grade ≥3) occurred in 4 patients (9%), and HAIP chemotherapy-related complications (Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events grade ≥3) occurred in 6 patients (13%). Biliary sclerosis occurred in 4 patients; 3 required stent placement. Conclusion: Adjuvant HAIP chemotherapy without systemic therapy did not achieve the hypothesized hDFS in patients undergoing repeat local treatment for recurrent CRLM.

items.title: Reirradiation After Repeat Breast Conserving Treatment: Contemporary Evidence, Technical Approaches, and Expert Recommendations
items.authors: Dorota Gabryś, Marianne Aznar, Arnaud Beddok, Eric D. Brooks, Dana Casey, J.Isabelle Choi, Stefanie Corradini, Reshma Jagsi, Dana Keilty, Anne Koch, Camilla Kronborg, Marcin Kubeczko, David McClatchy, Philip Poortmans, Marija Popovic, Danielle Rodin, Kilian E. Salerno, Simona F. Shaitelman, Manju Sharma, Yat Tsang, Linda Hong
items.abstract: Ipsilateral breast tumour event (IBTE) after previous breast conserving therapy (BCT) poses a therapeutic challenge. A considerable proportion of women will develop a recurrence or secondary tumour within a previously-irradiated breast over their lifetime. Historically, mastectomy has been the standard management for IBTE. However, repeat BCT followed by reirradiation has emerged as an alternative to mastectomy. Prospective and retrospective data confirm that a repeat BCT approach can achieve favourable local control with acceptable side effects in carefully selected women.

items.title: Closed-form, engine-portable uncertainty prediction of deformable image registration for dose accumulation in adaptive radiotherapy
items.authors: Ruggieri R, Bianchi N, Naccarato S, et al.
items.abstract: Voxel-level uncertainty estimates of the deformation vector field (DVF) produced by commercial deformable image registration (DIR) engines are flagged as an open issue by AAPM TG-132 but seldom available, preventing principled propagation into accumulated dose-volume histograms (DVHs). We propose and validate an engine-portable per-voxel σ predictor for the DVF (μ) of a deterministic DIR, calibrated by one scalar f against landmark Target Registration Error (TRE), with no access to the engine's internals.Approach. The framework combines (i) an anisotropic Gaussian correlation kernel, longer along the cranio-caudal axis, generalising the isotropic kernel of Smolders et al. (2023); and (ii) a heuristic-residual σ_h=f[wR̃+(1-w)d̃] (default w=0.7), where R̃ combines a self-similarity descriptor residual with an image-gradient suppression factor and d̃ is |Jacobian determinant-1|, both normalised to [0,1]; σ_h is closed-form, computed from the image pair and the DVF without optimisation or training. For each combination of dataset and DIR engine (a cell), f is calibrated against TRE via grid search minimising the Landmark Expected Calibration Error (LECE).Main results. Across 4 publicly annotated computed tomography datasets (Lung-, Abdominal- and Liver-DIR-QA and DIR-LAB Castillo; 44,778 landmarks) and 4 DIR engines (ANTs SyNRA, ConvexAdam, uniGradICON, Elastix), with f fitted on other patients (5-fold cross-validation), the calibrated σ_h achieves, in the per-direction convention of Smolders et al., LECE within or below their 0.41-1.34mm range in all 16 cells (cases with final root-mean-square TRE ≤10mm retained). A constant σ calibrated likewise also meets this range, but the variation of σ_h raises the held-out log-likelihood in 13 cells; σ_h ranks landmarks by error only weakly (Spearman ρ=-0.11 to +0.34).Significance. A one-scalar, post-hoc calibration yields voxel-level DVF uncertainty for any deterministic DIR that exports its DVF, partly addressing the AAPM TG-132 gap; propagation into accumulated DVH bands is illustrated on one lung stereotactic body radiotherapy case.

items.title: Mesh-based detailed human kidney models of the ICRP reference adults for radiopharmaceutical therapy dosimetry: microscale model of the renal cortex
items.authors: President B, Dawson RJ, Bolden Ii RE, et al.
items.abstract: Objective: Radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) is a rapidly evolving field in oncology, driven by advances in molecular targeting, such as prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA), and the use of radionuclides with different radiation emissions, including beta emitters and alpha emitters. RPT is typically used to treat disseminated cancers, where dosimetry-based treatment planning aims to limit radiation exposure to normal organs and reduce toxicity. This study aimed to develop a three-dimensional, histology-informed model of the human renal cortical labyrinth to support microscale dosimetry and the development of dose-response models for renal toxicity in RPT. The microscale model was dosimetrically coupled to an improved macroscale kidney model within the ICRP reference adult male and female phantoms. Approach: Histological human kidney sections were serially imaged using a high-resolution digital camera mounted on a light microscope. The images were imported into 3D Slicer for volumetric reconstruction. Renal corpuscles were manually segmented, and convoluted tubules were mapped using centerline luminal markers. Glomeruli were reconstructed by stitching segmented slices and scaling them to match diameters measured in 3D Slicer. Bowman's capsules were modeled to surround each glomerulus. Proximal and distal convoluted tubules (PCTs and DCTs) were created using a multi-pipe function. Main Results: The final microscale model included seven renal corpuscles with their respective PCTs and DCTs, embedded within a representative microenvironment containing tubule fragments, blood vessels, and extracellular tissue. Absorbed fractions were calculated for multiple source-target combinations. These microscale dosimetry results were coupled with corresponding macroscale kidney dosimetry to generate S-values for more than 1200 radionuclides. Significance: A three-dimensional, histology-informed model of the human renal cortical labyrinth was developed from H&E-stained kidney sections to represent the principal components of the nephron and its surrounding microenvironment. Coupling the microscale and macroscale models provides a framework for evaluating radionuclide-specific energy deposition at both spatial scales.

items.title: Mesh-based detailed human kidney models of the ICRP reference adults for radiopharmaceutical therapy dosimetry: macroscale models
items.authors: Shin B, Colon C, Choi C, et al.
items.abstract: Objective: In radiopharmaceutical therapy, the kidney is a major dose-limiting organ for many radiopharmaceuticals. The ICRP adult mesh-type reference computational phantoms (MRCPs) define the kidneys only with cortex, medulla, and pelvis regions, limiting the ability to characterize heterogeneous dose distributions within the kidneys. The present study aims to develop anatomically detailed macroscale kidney models for the adult MRCPs-comprising the capsule, cortex, medullary pyramids, papillae, pelvis wall, pelvis epithelium, and urine. Approach: The cortex, medullary pyramids, and papillae were constructed by segmenting 15 cadaveric kidney specimens and scaling them in accordance with the reference volumes and location, whereas the capsule, pelvis wall, pelvis epithelium, and urine were constructed based on target thicknesses. The developed models were integrated into the MRCPs and implemented in PHITS Monte Carlo code to compute absorbed fractions and specific absorbed fractions (SAFs) for photons, electrons, and alpha particles. The S values for clinically relevant therapeutic and diagnostic radionuclides were then derived using the SAF dataset and the ICRP Publication 107 decay data. Main Results: Anatomically detailed macroscale kidney models were developed for the adult male and female in a tetrahedral mesh format. The total masses were matched to the ICRP reference masses within 0.1% deviation. Compared with the original MRCP kidneys, the new kidney models produced substantial differences in SAFs, particularly for source-target combinations involving the renal pelvis, reflecting the more anatomically detailed representation of the collecting system. These differences resulted in corresponding differences in S values, depending on the radionuclide and source-target combination. Significance: The developed kidney model and established dataset enable subregional dose assessment within the kidney for radiopharmaceutical therapy dosimetry. This capability facilitates evaluation of heterogeneous dose distributions among kidney substructures and may support optimization of administered activity in treatment planning.

items.title: Social Deprivation, not Rurality, is Associated with Receipt of Guideline-concordant Care for Pancreatic Cancer in North Carolina, USA
items.authors: Ouellette S, Kim K, Baggett CD, et al.
items.abstract: Introduction: Rural-dwelling patients with pancreatic cancer (PC) and a higher Social Deprivation Index (SDI) score may be less likely to receive guideline-concordant care (GCC) than patients living in urban areas. We hypothesized that SDI score and rurality would affect the receipt of GCC among patients with PC. Methods: The North Carolina Central Cancer Registry was queried to identify patients with PC from 2004 to 2019. GCC was defined by National Comprehensive Cancer Network guidelines for PC/Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results staging as localized disease (surgery/chemotherapy), regional disease (at least chemotherapy), or distant disease (chemotherapy and/or palliative care). Multivariable regression assessed the impact of patient-level factors, SDI score, and geographic location on the receipt of GCC. Results: The cohort included 3595 patients with PC: 2532 (70%) urban and 1063 (30%) rural dwellers. Most had regional disease at diagnosis (n = 1871; 52%), were aged 65-79 years (n = 2021; 56%), were female (n = 1891; 53%), were non-Hispanic white (n = 2619; 73%), and had a medium SDI score (n = 1767; 49%), a Charlson Comorbidity Index score of 0 (n = 987; 27.5%), and a Frailty Index of 3+ (n = 976; 27%). GCC was received by 151 (32%) patients with localized disease, 1533 (82%) with regional, and 886 (71%) with distant disease. Across all stages, high (odds ratio [OR] 0.71; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.55-0.92) and medium (OR 0.82; 95% CI 0.67-1.00) SDI scores were associated with a decreased likelihood of receiving GCC. Among localized patients, those with high (OR 0.43; 95% CI 0.21-0.85) and medium (OR 0.47; 95% CI 0.27-0.81) SDI scores had decreased GCC. There was no association between SDI score and GCC among patients with regionalized and distant disease. Across all stages, there was no association between GCC and geographic location. Conclusion: Social deprivation, not rurality, was associated with a decreased receipt of GCC for patients with PC. Multilevel interventions are needed to modify barriers and facilitators of GCC receipt at a state level.

items.title: BEHOLD phase 3 clinical development program of mocertatug rezetecan in ovarian and endometrial cancer
items.authors: Hurteau J, Grayeski M, Dixon J
items.abstract: Mocertatug rezetecan (Mo-Rez; GSK5733584) is a B7-H4-targeting antibody-drug conjugate comprising a humanized anti-B7-H4 monoclonal antibody linked to the topoisomerase I inhibitor rezetecan. In the Phase 1 BEHOLD-1 study (NCT06431594), Mo-Rez demonstrated encouraging antitumor activity in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer (objective response rate [ORR], 62%) and recurrent/advanced endometrial cancer (ORR, 67%), supporting further clinical evaluation in Phase 3 studies. The global BEHOLD Phase 3 clinical program consists of five randomized studies evaluating Mo-Rez across ovarian and endometrial cancer treatment settings, with approximately 3,070 patients planned for enrollment. The ovarian cancer studies evaluate platinum-resistant disease (BEHOLD-Ovarian01, NCT07286266), platinum-sensitive disease (BEHOLD-Ovarian02, NCT076684612), and first-line maintenance for non-homologous recombination deficient disease (BEHOLD-Ovarian03, NCT07694427). The endometrial cancer studies evaluate previously treated advanced/recurrent disease (BEHOLD-Endometrial01, NCT07286331) and first-line maintenance for mismatch repair proficient disease (BEHOLD-Endometrial02, NCT07684599). Primary endpoints include progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS), depending on study design. Secondary and exploratory endpoints include safety, pharmacokinetics, biomarkers, immunogenicity, and quality-of-life assessments. Collectively, the BEHOLD program evaluates three therapeutic strategies: replacement of conventional chemotherapy with a B7-H4-directed ADC, combination approaches with bevacizumab or immune checkpoint inhibitors, and use of Mo-Rez as maintenance therapy. Tumor tissue collection across studies enables prospective evaluation of B7-H4 expression and other biomarkers as predictors of clinical benefit. The BEHOLD program represents a comprehensive Phase 3 clinical development effort designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of Mo-Rez across multiple ovarian and endometrial cancer settings and to further characterize the clinical relevance of B7-H4 as a therapeutic target in gynecologic malignancies.

items.title: [Review] Lynch syndrome
items.authors: Neil A J Ryan, Richard Gallon, Terri McVeigh, Kevin J Monahan, Gabriela Moeslein, David N Church, Mev Domínguez-Valentin, Tracy Smith
items.abstract: Lynch syndrome is the most common inherited cancer predisposition syndrome, affecting approximately one in 350–450 individuals, yet the majority of carriers remain undiagnosed, representing a substantial and preventable public health burden. Caused by germline pathogenic variants in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes, Lynch syndrome confers markedly elevated and heterogeneous risks of colorectal, endometrial, and multiple extracolonic cancers. Advances in molecular diagnostics, particularly universal tumour testing for MMR deficiency, have transformed case identification and enabled targeted germline testing and cascade screening of relatives at risk.

items.title: Diagnostic Performance of Nectin-4-targeted [(68)Ga]Ga-DOTA-N188 PET/CT versus [(18)F]-FDG PET/CT for Staging of Locally Advanced and Metastatic Urothelial Carcinoma: A Prospective, Single-center, Phase 2 Feasibility Trial
items.authors: Laukhtina E, Muin D, Spielvogel CP, et al.
items.abstract: Enfortumab vedotin (EV), an anti-nectin-4 antibody-drug conjugate, alone and with pembrolizumab (EV plus pembrolizumab [EV/P]), has transformed the treatment of locally advanced/metastatic urothelial carcinoma (la/mUC), yet remains biomarker agnostic. We prospectively evaluated [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-N188 PET/CT ([68Ga]-N188 PET/CT) as a whole-body alternative for nectin-4 imaging, with [18F]-FDG PET/CT as an active comparator and conventional computed tomography as the reference standard for staging la/mUC in 25 patients planned for EV/P. [18F]-FDG PET/CT showed a higher maximum standardized uptake value and tumor-to-background ratio than [68Ga]-N188 PET/CT across most lesion types (primary tumor, visceral, and osseous), except for lymph nodes. The overall tracer correlation was weak (Spearman r = 0.196), strongest in lymph nodes (r = 0.657), and absent in primary tumors and bone lesions. For primary tumor detection, [68Ga]-N188 PET/CT had higher specificity (86% vs 57%) and positive predictive value (92% vs 83%) than FDG, which had higher sensitivity (88% vs 67%). Nodal staging performance was similar in the tracers. For distant metastases, both achieved 100% sensitivity and negative predictive value, with [68Ga]-N188 PET/CT showing marginally higher specificity. [68Ga]-N188 PET/CT is feasible for whole-body nectin-4 assessment in la/mUC and supports a distinct biodistribution from FDG, suggesting complementary rather than interchangeable roles. Further prospective evaluation with treatment-outcome correlation is warranted before its use as a biomarker to guide EV-based therapy selection.

Antoine Eskander,

Ian Poon
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Purpose To evaluate the efficacy and safety of stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) in previously untreated primary mucosal head and neck cancer (HNC) patients unfit for conventional radiation therapy. Materials and Methods Retrospective analysis of previously unirradiated primary SCC mucosal HNC patients treated with SBRT from 2011 to 2022. Results HN SBRT was prescribed to 74 patients (median age: 81 years [52–97]; 85% ECOG 2–3) with 77 primary tumors (62% oral cavity; 64% T3‐4 disease). A five‐fraction prescription ranging from 35 to 50 Gy (95% received ≥ 40 Gy, 59.7% received ≥ 45 Gy) was delivered twice weekly, with the majority (81%) completing treatment within 14 days and all patients completing treatment. Symptomatic relief was achieved by 84%, including 27.3% with complete symptomatic response. With a median follow‐up of 7.3 months, 1‐year outcomes were 81% local control, 16% regional recurrence rate, and 12% distant metastasis rate. Median progression‐free and overall survival were 6.4 and 8 months, respectively. Acute Grade 3+ toxicity occurred in 36%, primarily mucositis (30%). Late Grade ≥ 3 toxicity was observed in 10% (n = 7), including osteoradionecrosis in 5 patients, with residual or concurrent disease present in 5% (n = 4). PTV > 159 cm3 was significantly correlated with late grade ≥ 3 toxicity (OR = 15.98; p = 0.0041). Conclusion High‐dose SBRT may deliver high rates of local control and palliation for primary mucosal HNC patients unfit for conventional radiation, but prospective, comparative, high‐quality data are needed. A randomized trial (NCT06641791) comparing SBRT to conventional palliative RT in the elderly unfit HNC patient is underway.

items.title: Treatment With the Shaker Head‐Lift Exercise in Head and Neck Cancer Patients With Radiation‐Induced Dysphagia: 12‐Month Results on Swallowing Function From a Randomized, Controlled Trial
items.authors:
Signe Rödseth Smith, 
Caterina Finizia, 
Kerstin Petersson, 
Lisa Tuomi
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Dysphagia is a common side‐effect after radiotherapy in head and neck cancer patients. This randomized study aimed to evaluate the effect of the shaker head‐lift exercise (HLE) after 12 months with flexible endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES). Methods Patients were randomly assigned to the intervention (n = 30) or the control (n = 31) group. The primary outcome was change according to the Penetration Aspiration Scale (PAS) at 12 months. Secondary outcomes included change according to the dynamic imaging grade of swallowing toxicity for flexible endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (DIGEST‐FEES) at 8 weeks and 12 months. Results The intention‐to‐treat analysis revealed no significant difference between the intervention and control groups regarding the change in the PAS score from baseline to 12 months. Swallowing safety improved significantly in the control group at the 8‐week follow‐up. Conclusions The HLE does not seem to improve swallowing function in individuals with radiation‐induced dysphagia.

items.title: Circulating tumor DNA to direct adjuvant immunotherapy across mismatch repair-deficient solid tumors
items.authors: Janjigian YY, Lumish MA, Foote MB, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Detection of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) harboring mutations that match those identified in resected tumor tissue signals occult residual disease after curative-intent surgery. Such patients are considered minimal residual disease (MRD)-positive and at high risk for recurrence and death. Few studies have shown that therapeutic intervention can alter recurrence risk in MRD-positive patients. We evaluated whether PD-1 blockade could reduce recurrence in MRD-positive patients with mismatch repair-deficient (dMMR) tumors after curative-intent resection regardless of tumor site of origin. Patients And Methods: We initiated a prospective phase II interventional study in patients who had undergone curative-intent resection of early-stage dMMR tumors from any anatomic site. Postoperative MRD status was assessed by first identifying those patients who had detectable ctDNA and then confirming the ctDNA relevance to MRD by matching mutations detected in ctDNA to somatic mutations detected in resected tumor tissue. Confirmed MRD-positive patients received 6 months of PD-1 blockade and were evaluated for ctDNA clearance and 24-month recurrence-free survival (RFS). MRD-negative patients underwent observation. Results: We screened 184 patients with early-stage dMMR solid tumors after curative resection and tumor sequencing with ctDNA testing for MRD assessment. Twenty-three patients (12.5%) were MRD-positive; after excluding one assigned to placebo and three with synchronous radiographic disease, 19 were eligible. Six developed recurrences before pembrolizumab initiation despite being disease-free at enrollment. The remaining 13 MRD-positive patients received 6 months of PD-1 blockade. ctDNA clearance at 6 months was achieved in 11 of 13 patients (85%). Five treated patients (38%) developed recurrence during follow-up. Median follow-up for the MRD-positive patients was 59 months (95% CI: 52-NR). Among 152 MRD-negative patients managed with observation, 14 (9%) developed recurrence during follow-up; 2-year RFS was 92%. Conclusions: These findings provide evidence that ctDNA-guided adjuvant therapy may offer clinical benefit in dMMR tumors regardless of tissue of origin.

items.title: Predicting efficacy and toxicity of drug combinations in salivary gland cancers: A model based on phase II trials
items.authors: Jiménez-Labaig P, Sanz-Beltran J, Forster MD, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Salivary gland cancers (SGCs) are rare and heterogeneous tumors lacking standard systemic treatment options in the recurrent/metastatic setting. Although clinical trials have shown activity of anti-HER2, chemotherapy, androgen receptor-targeted agents (ARTA) and androgen deprivation therapies (ADT), their combined effects remain largely unexplored. We aimed to model the potential outcomes of rational drug combinations to guide future clinical trial designs. Methods: Fifteen phase II trials were included, encompassing 524 patients (19% female, 81% R/M, 55% ductal, 11% adenocarcinoma, 5% mucoepidermoid). 7 trials assessed cytotoxic chemotherapy, 6 ARTA ± ADT, and 5 anti-HER2 therapies (3 as antibody-drug conjugates, ADCs). Overall response rate (ORR) and grade ≥ 3 treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) were estimated using Bliss and additivity models. Median progression-free survival and overall survival (OS) were reconstructed using parametric survival models. Results: Sixty combinations were assessed. In AR + HER2 + disease, triple combinations involving ARTA-ADT and anti-HER2-ADCs, or chemotherapy plus anti-HER2 yielded the highest predicted ORRs (94.5% by Bliss). In AR + HER2-, chemotherapy-based combinations and ARTA-ADT showed a greater relative ORR gain overall compared with AR + HER2+: +14.29(1.1-21.9) vs + 6.26(0.8-14.3). Estimated median 5- and 3-year OS was achieved in AR + HER2 + and AR + HER2- combinations respectively. Grade ≥ 3 TRAEs showed the highest rates in chemotherapy regimens (93.1 by Bliss, uncapped 126.5% by additivity) and lower toxicity with ADCs (23.3%, 24.8%). Conclusions: Predicted efficacy and safety outcomes highlight potential rational drug combinations that merit evaluation in future SGC clinical trials, ideally using a sequential approach, with particularly promising incremental benefit in AR + HER2- disease. Expected toxicity may constrain the feasibility of certain combination strategies.

items.title: Cemiplimab plus chemotherapy versus chemotherapy in non-small-cell lung cancer with PD-L1 ≥1%: 5-year update of EMPOWER-Lung 3 Part 2 results
items.authors: Gogishvili M, Makharadze T, Melkadze T, et al.
items.abstract: Background: EMPOWER-Lung 3 Part 2, a phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled study, demonstrated substantial survival benefits with cemiplimab plus chemotherapy versus placebo plus chemotherapy in patients with previously untreated advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) without EGFR, ALK, or ROS1 alterations. Here, we report 5-year results from the subgroup analysis of patients with programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression ≥1%. Patients And Methods: Eligible patients were randomized 2 : 1 to receive histology-specific platinum-doublet chemotherapy plus cemiplimab 350 mg or placebo every 3 weeks for up to 108 weeks. The primary endpoint was overall survival (OS); secondary endpoints included progression-free survival (PFS) and objective response rate (ORR). This analysis focuses on patients with PD-L1 ≥1% with 5-year follow-up (last patient last visit: 27 February 2025). Results: Of 327 patients with PD-L1 ≥1% (out of 466 in the overall study), 217 received cemiplimab plus chemotherapy and 110 received placebo plus chemotherapy. After median follow-up of 60.5 months, median OS for cemiplimab plus chemotherapy was 24.0 months [95% confidence interval (CI) 20.9-28.4] versus 12.1 months (95% CI 10.1-15.7) for placebo plus chemotherapy [hazard ratio (HR) 0.54, 95% CI 0.41-0.70, P < 0.0001); median PFS was 8.3 months (95% CI 6.7-10.8) versus 5.5 months (95% CI 4.3-6.2, HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.39-0.65, P < 0.0001), and the ORR was 48.4% versus 22.7%, respectively. Improved efficacy over placebo plus chemotherapy was observed across squamous and nonsquamous histologies, in both locally advanced and metastatic disease, and in patients with PD-L1 1%-49% and ≥50%. Grade ≥3 treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 48.8% of patients receiving cemiplimab plus chemotherapy versus 27.5% receiving placebo plus chemotherapy. No new toxicities were identified. Conclusions: First-line cemiplimab plus chemotherapy continued to show durable clinical benefit versus placebo plus chemotherapy after 5 years of follow-up in PD-L1-positive advanced NSCLC.

items.title: Comparison of whole-lung, physical-dose, and BED3-guided subregional multi-omics for predicting 3-month symptomatic radiation pneumonitis after lung cancer radiotherapy: a dual-center study
items.authors: Liu L, Wang S, Li X, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Region definition may influence radiation pneumonitis (RP) prediction, particularly when treatment schedules differ. We compared whole-lung, physical-dose subregional, and voxelwise biologically effective dose with α/β = 3 Gy (BED3)-guided strategies. The target outcome was grade ≥ 2 symptomatic RP within 3 months after lung cancer radiotherapy. Methods: This retrospective dual-center study included 246 patients between March 2023 and December 2025: 171 in a hospital-defined development cohort and 75 in the center-2 assessment cohort. The outcome was any grade ≥ 2 symptomatic RP recorded within 3 months after radiotherapy. Seven clinical, DVH, radiomic, dosiomic, and combined model specifications were evaluated within each region-design strategy. Development used repeated stratified 5 × 5 nested cross-validation and optimism correction based on 1000 bootstrap samples. All candidate models used the same outer and corresponding inner partitions and bootstrap resamples. Center 2 was excluded from model development and optimism correction and was used for center-specific out-of-sample performance assessment. Results: Forty-three patients developed grade ≥ 2 symptomatic RP (27/171 in development; 16/75 in center 2). Under shared resampling, center-2 AUCs for the complete whole-lung, physical-dose, and BED3 models were 0.676, 0.669, and 0.684, respectively. The differences were small, with overlapping confidence intervals. Across five intervals per representation, the highest point estimates were observed for physical dose 10-20 Gy (AUC 0.745) and BED3 ≥ 70 Gy3 (AUC 0.720). These interval rankings are exploratory and subject to selection optimism. Center-2 Brier scores for the complete models ranged from 0.184 to 0.260, compared with 0.168 for a constant-probability reference based on the center-2 event rate; calibration was inadequate for clinical use. Conclusions: The paired analysis did not identify a clearly superior region design. Complete-model center-2 AUCs differed by at most 0.015, with overlapping confidence intervals. Physical dose 10-20 Gy and BED3 ≥ 70 Gy3 produced the highest interval-level point estimates, but these rankings are exploratory. Recalibration and prospective multicenter validation are required before clinical use. Trial Registration: Not applicable.

items.title: Differential Impact of Postoperative Radiotherapy on Survival Across Clinical Treatment Score Post-5 Years Risk Categories in Early-Stage Luminal Breast Cancer After Breast-Conserving Surgery
items.authors: Li GQ, Kemu QLY, He XZ, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: To evaluate the role of Clinical Treatment Score post-5 years (CTS5) in stratifying post-operative radiotherapy (PORT) benefits in patients with T1-2N0, estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer (BC) after breast-conserving surgery (BCS). Methods: We included patients whose survival duration ≥ 60 months using the data from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results database. The association between CTS5 and survival was assessed. Results: A total of 23504 patients were included. The majority of patients (n = 19334, 82.3%) were classified as low CTS5, 3792 (16.1%) as intermediate CTS5, and 378 (1.6%) as high CTS5. The low CTS5 group exhibited significantly superior BCSS (P < .001) and OS (P < .001) than the intermediate and high CTS5 groups. While CTS5 was confirmed as an independent prognostic factor for breast cancer-specific survival (BCSS) and overall survival (OS), its interaction with PORT efficacy was paradoxical. Contrary to the hypothesis that higher-risk patients would derive the greatest benefit, the survival advantage of PORT was predominantly observed in the low CTS5 group, where PORT significantly improved both BCSS (P = .004) and OS (P < .001). Conversely, in patients with intermediate and high CTS5 scores, PORT did not confer a significant benefit regarding BCSS or OS. Conclusions: CTS5 serves as a robust independent prognostic indicator and a cost-effective tool for risk stratification. The benefit of PORT in early-stage BC is most pronounced in low CTS5 patients. These findings highlight the potential of CTS5 as a stratification tool for identifying differential PORT benefit, although its role in prospectively guiding PORT selection requires validation.

items.title: Stakeholder perspectives on simulation-based education in radiation oncology: opportunities and barriers
items.journal: Tech Innov Patient Support Radiat Oncol
items.authors: Kok M, Den Ouden MEM, Hertel IM, et al.
items.abstract: Radiation therapists (RTTs) face increasing clinical demands, limiting opportunities for structured training and feedback during work-based learning. This study explored whether simulation-based education (SBE) could address these challenges. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 16 stakeholders (i.e. students, RTTs, managers and educators) in a Dutch academic hospital. Participants valued SBE for providing a safe environment for repetitive practice, feedback and bridging theory and practice. Reported barriers included time, costs, resources and limited fidelity. Technical skills, methodical working and teamwork were seen as suitable learning objectives. The study concludes that successful SBE implementation requires institutional support, trained faculty and realistic, learner-centred scenarios.

items.title: Biological target volume and tumor spread map: A combined approach for advanced radiotherapy targeting in glioblastoma
items.authors: Abbasian P, Ryner L, McCurdy B, et al.
items.abstract: Abstract Background Glioblastoma (GBM) radiotherapy planning typically applies fixed margins from the Gross Tumor Volume (GTV) to define the Clinical Target Volume (CTV) and Planning Target Volume (PTV). This standardized approach ignores patient‐specific patterns of microscopic tumor spread and biological abnormalities, risking under‐treatment of infiltrated tissue and unnecessary exposure of healthy brain regions. Purpose To address this limitation, we extended our novel Tumor Spread (TS) mapping approach, which models microscopic infiltration along white matter tracts to generate personalized CTVs, by incorporating a Biological Target Volume (BTV), derived from advanced diffusion and perfusion MRI, into the model. We then compared three radiation treatment planning strategies: (1) GTV with standard fixed‐margin CTV and PTV, (2) GTV with a personalized CTV (pCTVG) and PTV (PTVG), and (3) BTV with a personalized CTV (pCTVB) and PTV (PTVB). Each was evaluated for feasibility of dose coverage, healthy tissue sparing, and recurrence overlap. Methods MRI data from 10 newly diagnosed GBM patients were used. BTVs were contoured using Fractional Anisotropy (FA), Apparent Diffusion Coefficient (ADC), and relative cerebral blood volume (rCBV) maps. TS maps were generated from both GTV and BTV. Virtual volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT) treatment plans were created for all three strategies. We compared target volumes, organ‐at‐risk (OAR) doses, and spatial overlap with recurrence regions identified in follow‐up imaging. Results Both pCTVG and pCTVB were consistently smaller than the standard CTV, offering reduced irradiated volume while preserving tumor coverage. The pCTVG and pCTVB spared 59% and 49% of the standard CTV margin volume, respectively. All virtual plans met clinical conformality thresholds, and mean doses to organs at risk (OARs) were lower with both personalized strategies. At follow‐up, 98% of the volume of recurrent tumor was included in the standard PTV, 95% in PTVG, and 97% in PTVB. Dose coverage of ≥80% was achieved in 99% of the recurrence volume with standard PTV, and in 98% with both PTVG and PTVB. Conclusion This study demonstrated the clinical feasibility and potential dosimetric benefits of MRI‐derived, biology‐informed personalized target volumes for radiotherapy planning of glioblastoma patients.…

items.title: Tangential volumetric modulated arc therapy reduces cardiac and contralateral low-dose exposure compared with continuous volumetric modulated arc therapy in postoperative breast radiotherapy
items.authors: Knöchelmann AC, Fischer M, Burchardt K, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: Tangential volumetric modulated arc therapy may combine rotational conformality with tangential beam geometry. We compared tangential with continuous-arc volumetric modulated arc therapy for postoperative breast radiotherapy with deliberately matched target coverage, focusing on cardiac and contralateral low-dose exposure. Material And Methods: Fifty-four patients were included in this paired planning study. For each patient, the clinically delivered tangential plan and a matched continuous-arc plan were evaluated. Target coverage was matched by clinical-target-volume D95% and planning-target-volume D2%. Dose-volume endpoints, low-dose area-under-the-curve metrics, delta dose-volume histograms, subgroup interactions, and mechanistic organ-equivalent-dose surrogates were evaluated. Results: Target coverage and homogeneity were comparable, while conformity was higher with tangential planning (p = 0.006). Tangential planning reduced mean heart dose from 1.34 to 1.17 Gy (p < 0.001), contralateral lung mean dose from 0.94 to 0.57 Gy, and contralateral breast mean dose from 1.16 to 0.76 Gy (both p < 0.001). Mechanistic organ-equivalent-dose surrogates were reduced by 37.0% for the contralateral lung and 32.7% for the contralateral breast. Exploratory interaction analyses did not identify statistically significant interactions by laterality, deep-inspiration breath hold, simultaneous integrated boost, or regional nodal irradiation. Conclusions: In a clinically heterogeneous paired cohort that included boost irradiation, regional nodal irradiation, and deep-inspiration breath hold, tangential volumetric modulated arc therapy reduced cardiac and contralateral low-dose exposure while preserving target coverage.

items.title: Functional lung avoidance planning with combined ventilation-perfusion imaging versus individual functional imaging in lung cancer radiotherapy
items.authors: Michimata G, Nakajima Y, Kimura T, et al.
items.abstract: Background And Purpose: Functional lung avoidance radiotherapy using four-dimensional computed tomography (4DCT) ventilation or single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) perfusion has been studied independently, however few studies have evaluated their combined use. The aim of this study was to examine whether integrating both modalities improved sparing of high functional lung (HFL) in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Materials And Methods: Forty-seven patients with NSCLC underwent 4DCT ventilation and SPECT perfusion imaging. One patient was excluded, leaving 46 for analysis. Functional lung maps were segmented into high, middle, and low functional lung. Four volumetric-modulated arc therapy (VMAT) plans using 6 MV photons per patient were generated: anatomical (A), ventilation-guided (V), perfusion-guided (Q), and combined ventilation-perfusion-guided (VQ). Dose-volume and dose-function metrics were compared among plans. Correlations between tumor proximity to HFL and dose reduction were assessed. Results: All function-guided plans significantly reduced HFL dose compared with A plans (p < 0.001). Among the function-guided plans, VQ plans yielded the lowest mean lung doses (MLDs) in high ventilated lung (VQ plans, 11.5 Gy; A plans, 12.4 Gy) and high perfused lung (VQ plans, 10.0 Gy; A plans, 11.1 Gy). Function-weighted metrics, including functional MLD, were also lowest with VQ plans, indicating improved functional lung sparing. Dose reduction correlated with tumor proximity to HFL, with the strongest associations observed at planning target volume expansions between 25 and 45 mm. Conclusions: Integrating 4DCT ventilation and SPECT perfusion into radiotherapy planning improved functional lung sparing compared with anatomical or single-modality planning. Tumor proximity to functional lung influenced the magnitude of dose-volume benefits.

items.title: Vitamin D supplementation, cancer incidence and mortality: Randomized trials revisited
items.authors: Wang Y, Sha S, Gwenzi T, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Vitamin D insufficiency and deficiency are highly prevalent among older adults globally and have been associated with increased cancer mortality in observational studies. Large randomized trials (VITAL and D-Health) found no reductions in cancer incidence or mortality with vitamin D supplementation but included mostly vitamin D-sufficient populations. Methods: Using UK Biobank (UKB) data, we conducted analyses informed by the VITAL and D-Health designs, applying their eligibility criteria and assuming the serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D) increases observed in the trials (30 and 38 nmol/L, respectively). Populations meeting the trial criteria were weighted to match the trial baseline 25(OH)D distributions. To emulate alternative targeted interventions, analyses were restricted to vitamin D-insufficient or -deficient individuals (25(OH)D < 50 or < 30 nmol/L, respectively). Multivariable Cox models estimated associations per 30 or 38 nmol/L higher baseline 25(OH)D concentration over the corresponding trial follow-up periods. Results: In analyses reflecting the original VITAL or D-Health 25(OH)D distributions, no association with cancer incidence or mortality was observed for the 25(OH)D increases achieved in the trials. However, inverse associations with cancer mortality were observed among vitamin D-insufficient and -deficient individuals, with hazard ratios (95% confidence intervals) of 0.93 (0.86-1.02) and 0.87 (0.77-0.97) in the VITAL-type cohort, and 0.92 (0.85-0.99) and 0.87 (0.80-0.96) in the D-Health-type cohort. Conclusion: Increases in 25(OH)D concentrations achieved in the trials were associated with substantially lower cancer mortality among vitamin D-insufficient and -deficient individuals. Null effects on cancer incidence and mortality observed in the trials were to be expected given the lack of associations between 25(OH)D and these outcomes among vitamin D replete populations.

items.title: Far Medial Endoscopic Transcervical Approach for Excision of a Recurrent Clival Chordoma Involving the Parapharyngeal and Prevertebral Spaces
items.authors: Kim JD, Brandel MG, Podury A, et al.
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Background and Importance Chordoma is a rare, malignant neoplasm arising from notochordal remnants. Addressing recurrent disease is challenging due to scar tissue formation, proximity to neurovascular structures, and altered clinical anatomy from prior surgery and/or radiation therapy. Herein, this work describes technical considerations and operative principles utilized in endoscopic transcervical resection for recurrent craniocervical chordoma extending into the right prevertebral/parapharyngeal space. Clinical Presentation A 16‐year‐old male with a history of clival chordoma was found to have an expansile mass spanning the C1‐C2 levels in the right prevertebral/parapharyngeal space on surveillance MRI. He had previously undergone definitive chemoradiation therapy as this tumor was initially misdiagnosed as rhabdomyosarcoma in another country at 13 years of age. He subsequently underwent multiple surgical procedures and treatments, including far lateral craniotomy with occiput‐to‐C2 posterior spinal fusion, combined endoscopic endonasal and transoral resection, and definitive proton therapy at our institution. An endoscopic transcervical approach was selected for salvage surgery as this provided an unoperated corridor with direct access to the neoplastic focus. The patient underwent uncomplicated gross total resection of recurrent chordoma. Conclusion This case demonstrates the safety and efficacy of far medial endoscopic neck dissection for recurrent craniocervical chordoma extending into parapharyngeal/retropharyngeal space in a pediatric patient. Key advantages of this approach include early identification and control of proximal great vessels and lower cranial nerves, dynamic visualization, bimanual surgical technique, and low risk of suboptimal wound healing by avoiding previously operated and/or irradiated tissue.

items.title: [Comment] Genomically matched targeted therapy for ovarian clear cell carcinoma

items.abstract: Ovarian clear cell cancer is a biologically distinct and clinically aggressive ovarian cancer subtype, representing approximately 20–25% of ovarian cancers in the Asia-Pacific region. Its genomic landscape is characterised by a predominantly homologous-recombination deficiency-negative phenotype, with recurrent alterations in ARID1A (40–50%) and PIK3CA (30–40%), suggesting a biology driven by epigenetic dysregulation or oncogenic signalling, rather than genomic instability.1 Prospective studies dedicated to ovarian clear cell cancer are scarce, and no biomarker-informed therapeutic strategy has yet successfully translated into an effective, genomically matched approach.

items.title: Safety and efficacy of transurethral resection of the prostate before external beam radiotherapy in patients with prostate cancer and lower urinary tract symptoms
items.authors: Vrij C, Bruins HM, Rademakers K, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: To describe the safety and efficacy of planned transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) prior to external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) in patients with prostate cancer and lower urinary tract symptoms. Materials And Methods: Patients who underwent TURP ≤9 months before EBRT between March 2015 and March 2025 were included in this multicentre retrospective cohort. Urinary adverse events (UAE) were graded using Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 6. Cumulative incidence of grade ≥2 and ≥3 UAE was estimated with the Aalen-Johansen method with dead as a competing event, and associations with UAE after EBRT were explored with multivariable Cox regression. International Prostate Symptom Scores (IPSS) were analysed with linear mixed effects models. Results: A total of 200 patients were included. Median follow-up after EBRT was 30 months among patients without a grade ≥3 UAE. The cumulative incidence at 36 months after EBRT was 53% (95% CI 46 - 61) for grade ≥2 and 14% (95% CI 9.1 - 20) for grade ≥3 UAE. A longer TURP-EBRT interval was associated with grade ≥2 UAE (hazard ratio 1.18 per month, 95% CI 1.03 - 1.36), likely reflecting confounding by indication. A larger clinical target prostate volume was associated with a lower risk of grade ≥3 UAE (HR 0.95 per mL, 95% CI 0.92 - 0.99). The estimated mean IPSS decreased from 19.8 before to 11.1 after TURP and remained close to or below this level after EBRT. Conclusions: Pre-EBRT TURP is feasible, with manageable but clinically relevant urinary toxicity. Symptom improvement is maintained after EBRT. These findings support its use as a de-obstructive strategy in patients with prostate cancer and lower urinary tract symptoms requiring EBRT.

items.title: Risk Factors for Osteoradionecrosis After Head and Neck Radiotherapy: A Systematic Review
items.authors: Le Guevelou J, Larnaudie A, Biau J, et al.
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Introduction Although intensity‐modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) has led to a significant reduction in mandibular osteoradionecrosis (ORN) rates, head‐and‐neck radiotherapy (RT) is rapidly evolving—with increasing use of altered schedules and with novel systemic regimens including immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI). The aim of this work is to systematically review the established risk factors for ORN after head‐and‐neck RT and to provide a narrative outlook on emerging risk factors. Material and Methods A systematic review of the literature was performed in September 2025 on three databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase and Scopus), using the MeSH terms “osteoradionecrosis” and “head and neck neoplasm.” No language restriction was applied. Studies deemed eligible were studies reporting factors associated with the onset of osteoradionecrosis after photon‐based head‐and‐neck RT. Results A total of 14 articles were included (1 prospective, 13 retrospective). The proportion of patients who developed ORN ranged from 1.8% to 19.8%, with a median interval from RT to ORN onset of 8 to 40 months. Pre‐RT dental extraction (particularly within 7 days before RT start) and higher mandibular dose‐volume parameters (V50Gy, V60Gy, dose to the primary site) were consistently associated with ORN onset. Smoking was associated with a shorter time to ORN onset, and bone surgery with resection of the periosteum was a strong independent risk factor (HR 5.87). No included study reported altered fractionation (accelerated, hyperfractionated) as being a risk factor to develop ORN. Conclusion Risk factors for ORN include both patient‐related (smoking) and treatment‐related (pre‐RT dental extraction, mandibular V50Gy/V60Gy) parameters. Whether these risk factors retain their relevance in modern altered‐fractionation schedules and in ICI‐combination regimens is currently unknown and warrants dedicated analysis from prospective studies.

items.title: Palbociclib, Fulvestrant, Trastuzumab, and Pyrotinib for Patients with Advanced Breast Cancer with Brain Metastases: A Prospective Multicenter Phase 2 Trial
items.authors: Chen D, Wang N, Xu F, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Patients with hormone receptor-positive (HR+)/human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-positive (HER2+) advanced breast cancer (ABC) face a high risk of brain metastases (BMs), yet prospective systemic‑treatment evidence for this subgroup is limited. We conducted a multicenter, single-arm, phase 2 trial evaluating a chemotherapy-sparing regimen of palbociclib, fulvestrant, trastuzumab, and pyrotinib in patients with HR+/HER2+ ABC and measurable BMs. The interim analysis suggested preliminary intracranial activity with manageable toxicity. Methods: Eligible patients had HR+/HER2+ ABC with measurable BMs and no prior local treatment to the target lesion. The regimen was administered until progression, unacceptable toxicity, or death. The primary endpoint was confirmed central nervous system objective response rate (CNS-ORR). Secondary endpoints included overall ORR, progression-free survival (PFS), CNS-PFS, overall survival (OS), and safety. We present the final analysis for 32 enrolled patients. Results: From Dec 2020 to Feb 2026, 32 patients were enrolled. For 29 response‑evaluable patients, confirmed CNS‑ORR was 58.6% (95%CI 40.7‑74.5) and overall ORR 62.1% (95%CI 44.0‑77.3). With median follow‑up of 32.5 months, median CNS-PFS was 9.6 months (95% CI: 5.3-13.9), and median overall PFS was 12.3 months (95% CI: 6.8-17.7). OS remained immature (5 deaths; 24‑month‑OS rate 80.7%). Post‑hoc analyses suggested numerically better PFS/CNS‑PFS in chemotherapy‑naïve patients, whereas prior trastuzumab did not impair efficacy. Frequent grade ≥3 adverse events comprised diarrhea (37.5%), neutropenia (28.1%) and leukopenia (15.6%), with no treatment‑related deaths. Conclusions: The chemotherapy-sparing quadruple regimen showed promising intracranial activity, systemic disease control, and manageable toxicity in HR+/HER2+ ABC patients with BMs.

items.title: SPROUT Guidelines for Molecular Profiling for Children with Solid Tumors: A Consensus Recommendation from the American Association for Cancer Research
items.authors: Gestrich C, Furtado LV, Biegel J, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Molecular diagnostics are standard of care for most adults with solid malignancies, but implementation in pediatric solid tumors remains inconsistent. The SPROUT (Somatic Profiling for Pediatric Cancer Refining our Understanding and Treatment) Molecular Guidelines Working Group was convened to develop molecular testing guidelines for pediatric solid tumors. Experimental Design: A structured literature review was performed using Covidence to identify relevant clinical studies evaluating molecular diagnostics in pediatric solid tumors. The literature and collective clinical experience of the multidisciplinary working group were used to develop consensus recommendations for molecular profiling at diagnosis and at relapse or recurrence. Results: Of 361 manuscripts screened, 41 studies were included for data extraction. Based on the available evidence and expert consensus, recommendations were developed for the use and timing of DNA and RNA next-generation sequencing and methylation profiling across pediatric solid tumors. Conclusions: The SPROUT Molecular Guidelines provide a framework for standardized implementation of molecular diagnostics in pediatric solid tumors. Broad adoption of these recommendations may improve diagnostic precision, reduce variability in molecular testing, and increase opportunities for biomarker-directed therapy and clinical trial enrollment for children with cancer.

items.title: Local Consolidative Radiotherapy Combined With Immunochemotherapy for De Novo Metastatic Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma: A Meta‐Analysis
items.authors:
Li Ma, 
Fangmeng Fu, 
Wenxi Wang, 
Yangmei Zhou, 
Jianghu Zhang, 
Sufang Qiu
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Immunochemotherapy is the standard care of newly diagnosed metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). Limited trials with small sample sizes reported the potential benefit of delivering radiotherapy in these patients. The purpose of our systematic review and meta‐analysis was to examine the efficacy and toxicity of local consolidative radiotherapy when combined with immunochemotherapy as the first‐line treatment in newly diagnosed metastatic NPC, providing a reference for clinicians to make the best choice in clinical practice. Methods A comprehensive search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Medline, and CNKI to identify published literature between January 1, 2004 and June 30, 2025 to identify potential eligible studies, including patients with pathologically confirmed de novo metastatic NPC treated with radiotherapy and immunochemotherapy. Toxicity rates, progression‐free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS) for the endpoints of interest were extracted from the articles, and the 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated. The systematic review and meta‐analysis were conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 Statement, and the study protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD42024607034). Results Seven studies with a total of 802 patients were analyzed to evaluate the efficacy and toxicity of first‐line local radiotherapy and immunochemotherapy in newly diagnosed metastatic NPC. The results showed that the addition of consolidative radiotherapy to immunochemotherapy significantly improved PFS in de novo metastatic NPC (HR = 0.48 [0.38, 0.60]) using a fixed‐effects model (I 2 = 44%, p = 0.15). The random‐effects pooled result indicated that consolidative radiotherapy added to immunochemotherapy failed to improve OS (HR = 0.52, 95% CI: 0.18–1.61, I 2 = 59%, p = 0.12). The pooled event rates of toxicities are 62.52% (95% CI: 25.22%–92.73%, I 2 = 97.8%), 63.03% (95% CI: 29.6%–90.6%, I 2 = 97.2%), 57.54% (95% CI: 30.72%–82.15%, I 2 = 95.6%), 21.29% (95% CI: 8.08%–39.37%, I 2 = 91.2%), 7.12% (95% CI: 0.33%–21.55%, I 2 = 87.1%) for mucositis, dermatitis, xerostomia, ear toxicity, and trismus of all grades, respectively. Grade 3–4 mucositis, dermatitis, xerostomia, ear toxicity, and trismus were 9.57% (95% CI: 3.37%–18.49%, I 2 = 79.4%), 3.5% (95% CI: 1.87%–5.63%, I 2 = 19.3%), 0.39% (95% CI: 0.01%–1.29%, I 2 = 37.4%), 1.37% (95% CI: 0.01%–4.95%, I 2 = 69.3%), and 0.26% (95% CI: 0%–1.25%, I 2 = 0%), respectively.…

items.title: Timing of Postoperative Radiotherapy and Outcomes in Oropharyngeal Squamous Cell Carcinoma
items.authors:
Ismail M. Khaderi, 
David Strum, 
Nazineen Kandahari, 
Ahmad J. Odeh, 
Annie X. Wang, 
Abdullah W. Saleh, 
Trevor G. Hackman
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Timely postoperative radiotherapy (PORT) is recommended for head and neck cancer, but adherence and its impact in oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) remain unclear. Methods A retrospective cohort study of 3723 adults with OPSCC undergoing surgery (2015–2025) in the TriNetX US Collaborative Network was performed. Patients receiving PORT were compared by timing (< 6 weeks vs. 6–12 weeks) using propensity score matching. A 5‐year mortality and salvage surgery were assessed from a 6‐week landmark. Results In total, 69.3% initiated PORT within 6 weeks, with increasing compliance over time. After matching (n = 1108 per group), delayed PORT was associated with higher mortality (RR = 1.27, 95% CI = 1.06–1.54) and salvage surgery (RR = 1.46, 95% CI = 1.10–1.94). The greatest risk was observed with delays of 10–12 weeks. Conclusions Delayed PORT is associated with worse OPSCC outcomes, supporting efforts to minimize treatment delays. Although guideline adherence has improved, the optimal compliance threshold remains uncertain.
