items.title: Clinical dosimetry for nose vestibule carcinoma interventional radiotherapy (modern brachytherapy): 15 year's experience from a large tertiary center
items.authors: Fionda B, Rosa E, Parrilla C, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Nose vestibule carcinoma is a rare and often under-recognized clinical entity, with specific anatomical features that make treatment planning particularly challenging. Interventional radiotherapy (IRT, brachytherapy) represents a well-established organ-preserving treatment option, but its dosimetric characteristics remain insufficiently described. This study aimed to evaluate the temporal evolution of IRT for nose vestibule carcinoma over a 15-year period, focusing on implant technique, procedural complexity, and dosimetric parameters. Methods And Materials: Patients with nose vestibule carcinoma treated with high-dose-rate IRT at a single institution between 2012 and 2026 were retrospectively analyzed. Clinical target volume, number and anatomical distribution of catheters, and dose non-uniformity ratio were collected. Temporal trends and exploratory relationships between target volume, implant geometry, and dose heterogeneity were descriptively evaluated. Results: Eighty-five patients were included. The mean clinical target volume was 25 cc (range: 2.0-98.0 cc), while the mean number of implanted catheters was 10 (range: 3-25). The mean dose non-uniformity ratio was 0.53 (range: 0.30-0.78). Despite increasing implant complexity, the dose non-uniformity ratio progressively decreased, suggesting improved dose modulation and refinement of implant geometry. Conclusions: IRT for nose vestibule carcinoma evolved toward the treatment of larger and more complex targets while maintaining, and progressively improving, dosimetric quality. Overall, these findings suggest a progressive refinement of implantation and treatment-planning techniques with accumulated institutional experience.

Brachytherapy

items.title: Gynecologic hybrid and interstitial high-dose-rate brachytherapy
items.authors: Patel AK, Dare A, Horne ZD, et al.
items.abstract: Advances in high-dose-rate (HDR) brachytherapy techniques have improved local control and reduced morbidities associated with brachytherapy. Interstitial brachytherapy (ISBT) has traditionally been used for locally advanced gynecologic cancers not amenable to less invasive intracavitary brachytherapy (ICBT) techniques. The recent advent of hybrid brachytherapy (HBT) involves using modern brachytherapy applicators that combine intracavitary and interstitial components to optimize tumor target coverage and reduce normal tissue exposure. Given the importance of brachytherapy in the non-operative management of locally advanced gynecologic cancers, knowledge of and procedural competency with ISBT and HBT is crucial. However, gynecologic brachytherapy training during radiation oncology residency is variable, with significant gaps in experience and case numbers reported by resident trainees. The advent of HBT and ISBT may further exacerbate these gaps, as not all centers are equipped to provide training in high-quality HBT and ISBT. To this end, this article aims to summarize important concepts in ISBT and HBT, with a focus on cervical cancer, and to describe brachytherapy applicators, aspects of procedural competency, target delineation, treatment planning, and toxicity management.

items.title: Clinician Competencies for Self-Management Support in Cancer: Expert Consensus Recommendations From the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer
items.authors: Knowles R, Agbejule OA, Wallen M, et al.
items.abstract: Purpose: Many people affected by cancer benefit from self-management, but this requires support from cancer care clinicians. Currently, there is a lack of consensus about the minimum competencies required of clinicians to facilitate effective self-management support (SMS). Methods: A two-round online modified Delphi study involving cancer care clinicians was conducted to reach consensus on which performance criteria from a comprehensive SMS framework for cancer nurses should be considered minimum competencies that cancer care clinicians should possess. The perspectives of people affected by cancer regarding SMS needs were collected via online interviews and further shaped the statements. The project team finalized a list of minimum competencies for care-providers (care-provider version) and a reader-adjusted version for people affected by cancer (patient version). Results: 27 clinicians and 14 people affected by cancer participated. Eighteen performance criteria from the original framework reached consensus for inclusion as minimum competencies, with participant feedback informing refinements to both the care-provider and patient versions. The performance criteria included statements from all six domains of the original framework: person-centered and motivational communication, whole-person assessment of SMS needs and capacity, health promotion theories and interventions, coaching for behavior change tailored to the individual, monitoring and evaluating change in self-management behaviors and health outcomes, and quality improvement for integration of SMS in cancer care. Conclusion: The minimum competencies for SMS can be used to inform care provider education, skills assessment, and encourage patient activation for improved support, to optimize patient outcomes and health care utilization. International organizations, such as the Multinational Association for Supportive Care in Cancer, represent an ideal forum for the dissemination and strengthening of these competencies, and for local implementation.

items.title: Final analysis from PECATI phase 2 trial, lenvatinib in combination with pembrolizumab in pretreated advanced B3-thymoma and thymic carcinoma
items.authors: Remon J, Bironzo P, Girard N, et al.
items.abstract: Background: There is no standard second-line treatment for patients with platinum-refractory advanced B3-Thymoma (T) and thymic carcinoma (TC). In this population, the PECATI trial (NCT04710628) testing the combination lenvatinib and pembrolizumab met its primary endpoint, with 5-month progression-free survival (PFS) of 88.0%. Here we report the final clinical study results. Methods: PECATI is a single-arm, phase 2 trial enrolling patients with metastatic B3-T and TC, without autoimmune disorders that have progressed following at least one platinum-based chemotherapy. The trial evaluated lenvatinib (20 mg orally once daily) plus pembrolizumab (200 mg iv infusion once every 3 weeks) in 3-week cycles for a maximum of 35 cycles if no disease progression or toxicity. Results: 43 patients were enrolled: median age 57 years (33-81); 84% had a TC; 65% Masaoka Koga IVB, 51.2% of patients with ≥3 metastatic sites, and 44.2% received ≥2 prior lines for advanced disease. After a median follow-up of 24.6 months, the median PFS was 22.1 months (95%CI: 10.9-25.1), and the median overall survival (OS) was 40.2 months (95%CI: 19.1-not estimated), with 36-month OS rate of 53.0%. The confirmed ORR was 25.6% and median duration of response was not reached. The rate of grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events was 44.2% leading to treatment discontinuation in 27.9% of cases. Two (4.7%) non-treatment-related grade 5 events were reported. The rate of grade 3 immune-related adverse events was 11.6%. Conclusion: The final results of PECATI trial supports the combination lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab as a potential treatment option in pre-treated advanced B3-thymoma and thymic carcinoma. Toxicity profile is manageable but close monitoring is advised.

items.abstract: Recurrence remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality after curative-intent treatment of stage II–III colorectal cancer (CRC), including among patients receiving adjuvant chemotherapy. Recent randomized trials demonstrate that aspirin and structured exercise can further reduce recurrence risk and improve patient outcomes. Two phase 3 randomized trials provide evidence for extending adjuvant strategies beyond cytotoxic chemotherapy in CRC. In ALASCCA, 3 years of low-dose aspirin reduced recurrence by approximately 50% among patients with resected colon or rectal cancer harboring PI3K-pathway alterations, establishing a biomarker-guided approach to adjuvant aspirin therapy.

items.title: Eligibility and real-world use of adjuvant chemotherapy in colon cancer: a Dutch nationwide study
items.journal: JNCI: Journal of the National Cancer Institute Advance Access
items.abstract: Abstract Background Adjuvant chemotherapy (ACT) improves survival in patients with resected stage III and high-risk stage II colon cancer, yet its use in routine clinical practice remains variable. Real-world adherence to guideline-recommended ACT and factors influencing treatment use are not well defined at a population level. Methods In this nationwide population-based study, data from the Netherlands Cancer Registry (2005–2020) were used to identify adults with nonmetastatic colon cancer who underwent surgical resection. Eligibility for ACT was defined as pT4N0 or node-positive disease (pT1–3N+ or pT4N+) according to Dutch guidelines and the available NCR variables. Adherence, defined as initiation of ACT when eligible, and factors associated with it were analyzed, including age, comorbidity, tumor characteristics, hospital type and region, and the urgency of the primary tumor resection. Results Among 44,471 patients, 22,050 (49.6%) were pathologically eligible for ACT, of whom 12,748 (57.8%) initiated treatment. Among ineligible patients, 2.6% received ACT. Non-adherence was strongly associated with advanced age (29.9% of patients ≥75 without comorbidities received ACT), comorbidity, female sex, right-sided tumors, and non-elective surgery (all p < 0.001). Younger patients were more likely to receive ACT despite pathological ineligibility (p < 0.001). Adherence also varied by hospital type, with lower adherence in teaching and academic hospitals compared with general hospitals (p < 0.001). Conclusions In this nationwide cohort, guideline-recommended ACT was frequently not delivered to pathologically eligible patients. Adherence was influenced by several patient, tumor and hospital characteristics, highlighting factors associated with variation in guideline-based ACT receipt among colon cancer patients.

items.title: RTHistory: An automated tool for the extraction and presentation of radiotherapy course history for continuity of care applications
items.authors: Hink JB, Abdulkadir Y, Krupien A, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Transfer of radiation treatment records is a common task for radiotherapy clinics, as treatment history impacts future treatment planning, including prescription dose, fractionation, and normal tissue constraint selections. Currently, gathering radiation records relies on manual searches within treatment planning databases and Record and Verify (R&V) systems, a process that is time-consuming and subject to human error. Particularly challenging is discerning which plans were treated, and for how many fractions, in cases of treatment adaptation or early termination. Purpose: In this technical note, we present RTHistory, an open-source software tool that automates the extraction process for R&V systems that implement DICOM Query/Retrieve and summarizes the treatment history in a format optimized for efficient clinical readability and visual triage. Methods: RTHistory was configured to query multiple clinical systems through the DICOM protocol. The query process begins with downloading and analyzing the RTRecords, which document beam delivery. From these, internal DICOM object references are followed to gather the relevant planning files, including dose, simulation scan, and structure set. RTHistory then parses these DICOM files to create a treatment summary PDF report that describes the plan labels, prescription doses, treatment start and end dates, number of fractions treated, and a graphical representation of the dose washes of the treated plans. Rigorous software unit testing and error handling procedures were implemented to ensure reliability and accuracy of the extracted data. Results: RTHistory was evaluated on a clinical cohort of 61 patients comprising 177 distinct treatment plans across six anatomical sites from our institutional database, which included the ARIA/Eclipse R&V system and treatment planning system. Manual verification against clinical ARIA and Eclipse records confirmed 100% agreement in reconstructing delivered DICOM-RT objects (177/177 plans), with none of 439 undelivered plans included (specificity: 100%; 95% CI: 99.2%-100%). Performance testing for patients with at least one treatment planned in Eclipse (n = 51 patients) yielded a median overall patient run time of 115.4 s (aggregate per-plan: 59.5 s, 95% bootstrap confidence interval: 45.6-72.1 s), which scaled directly with the number of CT series (93.4 ± 20.0 s per series).…

items.title: A gait foundation model for prediction of multisystem health phenotypes from 3D skeletal motion
items.authors: Gabet A, Kohn S, Lutsker G, et al.
items.abstract: Gait is increasingly recognized as a vital sign, yet current approaches treat it as a symptom of specific pathologies rather than a systemic biomarker. Here we developed a gait foundation model for three-dimensional skeletal motion, which was recorded via a single-depth camera during 5 motor tasks, from 3,328 deeply phenotyped adults. Our purpose was to capture the full pattern of a person's movement and use it to predict health phenotypes such as grip strength and sleep quality across 18 body systems. Gait is conventionally described by engineered features (for example, calculated measurements such as cadence and stride length), which may fail to capture the fine detail of how a person moves. Our model instead translates movement into learned embeddings: sets of numbers that describe how all body joints move together over time. Learned embeddings outperformed engineered features for prediction of age (Pearson's r = 0.69), body mass index (r = 0.91) and visceral adipose tissue area (r = 0.83), and embeddings significantly predicted 1,887 of 3,210 tested phenotypes. Relative to a baseline model using age, body mass index, visceral adipose tissue and height alone, gait embeddings improved prediction in all 18 systems in males and 17 of 18 in females, as well as prediction of clinical diagnoses and medication use. Anatomical ablation analyses revealed that leg dynamics dominated metabolic and frailty predictions, and torso dynamics encoded sleep and lifestyle phenotypes. These findings establish gait as an independent, multisystem biosignal, motivating integration of gait analysis into routine clinical assessment as a scalable, passive vital sign.

items.title: Long-Term Survival After CRS-HIPEC for colorectal Cancer Peritoneal Metastases
items.authors: van Kesteren LJ, Aalbers AGJ, Chakroun A, et al.
items.abstract: Background: Most patients with colorectal cancer (CRC) and peritoneal metastases (PM) face a dismal prognosis. Cytoreductive surgery and hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (CRS-HIPEC) is a curative-intent treatment for patients with limited disease. This study assessed long-term survival and recurrence patterns. Methods: A consecutive cohort of patients with CRC-PM treated with CRS-HIPEC. Patients with complete macroscopic cytoreduction were eligible. Main outcomes were overall survival (OS), disease-free survival (DFS), peritoneal recurrence-free survival (PRFS) and recurrence patterns. Results: In total, 440 patients were evaluated over a median follow-up of 35.2 months (IQR 25.3-68.7). Induction systemic therapy was administered to 43.1% of patients. Median DFS was 9.7 months (95% CI 8.3-11.1), and median OS was 50.2 months (95% CI 44.3-56.2). Independent prognostic factors for decreased OS were Peritoneal Cancer Index (PCI) > 10, positive lymph node status (N-stage), ASA score > 2, and right-sided primary tumors. During follow-up, 71.4% of patients developed recurrent disease in the peritoneum (54.8%), lungs (22.9%), and liver (19.1%). Independent prognostic factors for decreased PRFS were lymph node metastases and higher PCI scores. Neither induction therapy nor HIPEC regimen was correlated with PRFS. Early metachronous presentation of peritoneal metastasis, also emerged as a significant adverse factor for OS, DFS and PRFS. Conclusions: Patients undergoing complete CRS-HIPEC achieved a favorable median OS exceeding 50 months, with approximately 30% of individuals exhibiting long-term survival indicative of cure. However, early recurrence remains a major problem and is in need for further research to improve CRS-HIPEC regimens.

items.title: Sampling-free Monte Carlo dropout approximation for single-pass uncertainty quantification in deep learning-based PET reconstructions
items.authors: Liu SZ, Zhang M, Bharkhada D, et al.
items.abstract: Medical image reconstructions using deep learning (DL) can rapidly generate high-quality images from degraded measurements, but their clinical adoption remains challenging, largely due to the lack of fast and reliable methods to quantify aleatoric (data-driven) and epistemic (model-driven) uncertainties on a per-prediction basis. We aim to develop a computationally efficient approach for estimating both uncertainties at the voxel level in DL-based image reconstruction within a single inference run.Approach: We present a moment propagation-based framework that analytically approximates the conventional, multi-realization Monte Carlo (MC) dropout by propagating feature-map means and marginal variances through network layers, followed by a pre-calibrated correction table to compensate for covariance effects omitted in the approximation. This enables joint estimation of reconstruction, aleatoric uncertainty and epistemic uncertainty in a single forward pass. The proposed framework was implemented on top of FastPET -- a network model synthesizing PET reconstructions from time-of-flight histo-images -- and evaluated in a patient pilot study of 26 total-body PET/CT acquisitions (16 [18F]-FDG and 10 [18F]-PSMA cases).Main Results: Proposed method achieved relatively strong agreement with the 50-pass MC approach, with absolute differences <0.5% for reconstruction, <4.2% for aleatoric uncertainty and <9.8% for epistemic uncertainty, along with narrow spreads across patients and tracer types, while reducing computation time by ~40-fold. In a complementary proof-of-concept low-count experiment, regional tracer uptake confidence intervals (CIs, derived from propagated uncertainties) widened with increased noise level, and reference uptakes consistently fell close to CI boundaries, indicating the proposed method could provide roughly calibrated uncertainty magnitudes reflecting quantitative prediction errors.Significance: The proposed approach provides a sampling-free and relatively accurate approximation to the multi-pass MC-based uncertainty estimation in the histo-image-based DL PET reconstruction framework. Per-prediction uncertainty quantification enables direct assessment of AI confidence and potentially supports more reliable and informed decision-making.

items.authors: Zhe Wang, Rebecca Watters, Lorna Roden, Gurdeep Mannu, Sileida Oliveros, David Dodwell
items.abstract: Management decisions when end of life is approaching are difficult and there are few studies addressing this concern using national cancer data. We conducted a retrospective population-based cohort study using linked English cancer registration, treatment and hospital records. We included 10,835 patients with pancreatic cancer who had received systemic anticancer therapy at some point, and had died during 2015-2019 and considered receipt of disease-targeted treatment (major surgery, radiotherapy or chemotherapy).
